lessons.title: What is Ideology?
lessons.notes_html:
An ideology is a collection of principles, beliefs and values that influence the worldview of an individual or a group. It affects their attitudes and opinions and provides information for their political, social, economic and moral stances. Ideologies work as conceptual structures through which we interpret reality, understand society's problems and propose remedies for them.

Types of Ideology

  • Most of the time, an ideology is based on politics, economics, religion, culture and societal conventions.
  • Well-known examples of ideologies are nationalism, religion, feminism, capitalism and socialism.
  • Ideologies may be obvious or hidden, but they strongly affect human conduct, decision-making and the identity of individuals and groups.

Importance of Ideology

  • Ideology influences a nation's governance structure, policy direction and societal values.
  • It affects political systems, economic policies, social and cultural values, and even foreign relations and healthcare.
  • It serves as a compass for a nation's aspirations and decides its identity — promoting unity among citizens, or inciting discord.
  • In democratic societies it shapes public discussion and elections; in authoritarian regimes it may be used to solidify authority.

Key Points

  • An ideology is a set of principles, beliefs and values that guides a person or a group.
  • Nationalism, religion, feminism, capitalism and socialism are well-known ideologies.
  • Ideology is the compass that decides a nation's identity, governance and direction.

lessons.title: Ideology of Pakistan and Islam
lessons.notes_html:
The ideology of Pakistan originated from the South Asian Muslim community's deep desire to preserve their distinctiveness within society. The Muslims believed that Hinduism and Islam are not merely two religious systems, but also two social institutions that have given rise to two unique cultures.

Two Different Social Orders

  • The divisions between Hindus and Muslims extend beyond politics — they are a confrontation of two distinct social structures.
  • The two nations cultivated distinct cultures and traditions despite having coexisted for over a millennium.
  • Their architecture, script, musical preferences and eating customs are all different.

Ideology of Pakistan and Islam

  • The ideology of Pakistan is based on Islamic values.
  • The Muslim nation was not founded upon any linguistic, ethnic, territorial or racial distinction — its members shared the faith of Islam.
  • Muslims demanded a sovereign state in the regions where they were in majority, so they could govern their lives according to the Holy Quran and the Sunnah.
  • Islam emphasises justice and equity, religious freedom, and equality for all citizens regardless of caste, sect, religion or region.
  • Cultural and religious tolerance, human rights, the rule of law and the dignity of humans are part of this ideology — and became part of the different constitutions enacted in Pakistan.

Key Points

  • Pakistan's ideology grew from the Muslims' desire to preserve their separate identity.
  • Hinduism and Islam are two different social orders with different cultures.
  • The ideology of Pakistan rests on Islamic values: justice, equality, tolerance and rule of law.

lessons.title: Economic and Social Deprivations of Muslims in India
lessons.notes_html:
During British rule, the Muslims encountered hardships that stemmed from historical circumstances and colonial policies. These included both economic and social deprivations, and they became an important reason why Muslims began to think of their own separate state.

Economic Deprivation

  • British economic policies aimed at strengthening the colonial administration and frequently resulted in the depletion of India's resources, which hit the Muslims especially hard.
  • The land tenure system changed with the Zamindari system, which displaced a significant number of Muslim cultivators.
  • Muslims were deprived of employment and educational opportunities, which increased economic disparities.

Social and Educational Deprivation

  • The educational policies of the British administration discouraged Arabic and Persian and focused on the English language.
  • Lack of education stopped Muslims from competing for specialised occupations and economic opportunities.
  • The Hindi-Urdu Controversy of 1867, which followed the unsuccessful War of Independence of 1857, was a major Hindu challenge to Muslim legacy and heritage; Hindus saw Urdu as the language of Muslims and prejudice against it arose.
  • Workplace discrimination was widespread — in hiring, the British frequently favoured Hindus, so Muslims felt politically excluded and remained under-represented in administrative and economic institutions.

Key Points

  • Colonial policies depleted India's resources and displaced Muslim cultivators through the Zamindari system.
  • British education policy discouraged Arabic and Persian and favoured English, leaving Muslims backward.
  • Job discrimination and political exclusion pushed Muslims to demand a separate state.

lessons.title: Quaid-e-Azam and Allama Iqbal on the Ideology of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was instrumental in establishing the ideology of Pakistan. Through his speeches he clearly communicated that the Muslims of the Subcontinent were a separate nation that could survive only if granted a separate homeland, where they could practise their beliefs without fear or pressure.

Quaid-e-Azam and the Ideology of Pakistan

  • Quaid-e-Azam ardently supported the Two-Nation Theory: Hindus and Muslims were separate nations with distinct religious, cultural and social identities.
  • Addressing the Punjab Muslim Students Federation on March 2, 1942, he said no honest man can dispute that the Muslims are a nation by themselves, distinctly separate from the Hindus.
  • In his Lahore address of 1940 he said Islam and Hinduism are not religions in the strict sense, but different and distinct social orders that can never evolve a common nationality.
  • He placed great emphasis on equality and social justice — all individuals, irrespective of origin, should enjoy equal rights and opportunities.
  • On August 11, 1947 he explained: people are free to go to their places of worship; religion, caste or creed has nothing to do with the business of the State.
  • He also wanted Pakistan to maintain amicable relations with other countries, based on mutual respect and equality.

Allama Muhammad Iqbal and the Ideology of Pakistan

  • Allama Muhammad Iqbal is the ideological compass and lodestar of Pakistan — his orations and writings gave Pakistan's ideology its basis.
  • In his Allahabad Address of 1930 he presented the idea of a separate state for Muslims in South Asia: Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sind and Balochistan amalgamated into a single State.
  • The word Pakistan was not used in the address, but it is regarded as a milestone that led to the creation of Pakistan in 1947.
  • Iqbal emphasised an Islamic state that would preserve morality, equity and justice, with equitable distribution of resources and prohibition of interest.
  • In a 1937 letter to Quaid-e-Azam he wrote that for Indian Muslims the cultural problem was of much greater consequence than the economic problem.

Key Points

  • Quaid-e-Azam presented Muslims as a separate nation through the Two-Nation Theory.
  • His August 11, 1947 address promised equal citizenship and religious freedom to all.
  • Iqbal's Allahabad Address of 1930 first proposed a single Muslim state in the north-west.

lessons.title: British Colonialism and Its Impact
lessons.notes_html:
British colonialism refers to the system of governance and control that the British established over various territories and countries around the world, particularly in the 18th and 19th centuries. These countries included Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India and many others.

British Colonialism in India

  • In India, British colonialism started in the 17th century with the establishment of the East India Company, which gradually expanded its control over the subcontinent.
  • British rule in India lasted until 1947, when India gained its independence.
  • Positive impacts included modern infrastructure and institutions, the spread of education and a modern legal system.
  • Negative impacts were far more long-lasting: exploitation of local resources, unfair economic policies, widespread poverty and inequality, displacement of indigenous populations, destruction of cultural heritage and divisive policies that fuelled communal tensions.

Exploitation of Resources

  • The main reason behind exploitation was the British desire to extract maximum profit from the colonies.
  • They imposed high taxes and tariffs on local industries, forcing them to export raw materials instead of developing manufacturing — creating a cycle of dependency on foreign markets.
  • India's thriving textile industry declined when cheap, machine-made British textiles flooded the Indian market; local weavers became unemployed and impoverished.

Divide and Rule Policy

  • Under divide and rule, the British supported Hindus over Muslims in almost every field, which increased tensions, mistrust and animosity between the two communities.
  • Colonial rule also had a psychological impact — it created a sense of inferiority and dependency among the people.
  • The British prioritised cash crops for export over food crops, which often led to famines; heavy revenue taxes burdened farmers and caused widespread rural poverty.

Key Points

  • Colonialism began in India with the East India Company in the 17th century and ended in 1947.
  • Its negative effects — resource exploitation, poverty and communal division — lasted longer than its benefits.
  • Divide and rule favoured Hindus over Muslims and destroyed inter-religious harmony.

lessons.title: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement
lessons.notes_html:
After the War of Independence, reformers tried to uplift the Muslims. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan convinced Muslims to get modern education to come out of the darkness of illiteracy and poverty.

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan

  • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was born in Delhi in 1817. His education covered the Quran and several scientific disciplines — mathematics, medicine, Persian, Arabic and Urdu.
  • After the unsuccessful War of Independence of 1857, Muslims faced atrocities because the British blamed them as the main cause of the event.
  • Sir Syed wrote Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (The Causes of the Indian Revolt), attributing the uprising mainly to British ignorance and their assertive policies of expansion.
  • His interaction with Western societies shaped his views — he recognised the importance of Western-style education for Muslims to acquire new knowledge and keep pace with contemporary developments.

Aligarh Movement

  • The Aligarh Movement, led by Sir Syed in the 19th century, was a socio-educational movement to elevate the Muslim population of British India.
  • Its primary objective was to tackle educational underdevelopment among Muslims by promoting contemporary education, scientific expertise and practical understanding.
  • In 1875, Sir Syed established the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) College at Aligarh to integrate Western educational principles with Islamic studies.
  • The college later became Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) — still one of India's top universities, with an enrollment of more than 37,000 students.

Role of the Aligarh Movement in the Success of the Pakistan Movement

  • The movement laid the intellectual and educational foundation that significantly contributed to the Pakistan Movement.
  • AMU became a central hub of modern education, and its alumni assumed significant positions in social, political and economic fields.
  • It demanded separate electorates and equitable representation of Muslims in government and legislative bodies.
  • The concept of Muslims as a distinct political and cultural entity gained traction, establishing the groundwork for the Two-Nation Theory.

Key Points

  • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (born 1817, Delhi) urged Muslims to adopt modern Western education after 1857.
  • He founded MAO College at Aligarh in 1875, which later became Aligarh Muslim University.
  • The Aligarh Movement prepared the educated leadership and ideas behind the Pakistan Movement.

lessons.title: Simla Deputation, Muslim League and Early Reforms, 1906-1911
lessons.notes_html:
The years 1906 to 1920 saw a number of significant developments in the Pakistan Movement for an independent state for the Muslims of the subcontinent. After the unsuccessful War of Independence, the Muslims were under immense pressure and were deprived of their rights in almost every sphere. The Indian National Congress, formed in 1885, was seen at first as protecting the rights of all Indians, but its policies made it clear that it represented only the Hindu majority.

Simla Deputation 1906

  • After the Liberal Party victory in the 1905 English elections, constitutional reforms were promised for India, so the Muslims decided to present their demands through the Simla Deputation.
  • The deputation was a group of thirty-five Muslim leaders from every province of India. It met Viceroy Lord Minto in 1906 and was led by Agha Khan and Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk.
  • Its main demands were separate electorates for Muslims, reserved seats in legislative councils, adequate representation in government service, assurance that reforms would not harm Muslim political, educational and social rights, appointment of Muslim judges, and university status for MAO College.
  • The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 partially accepted these demands, and the deputation later led to the formation of the All-India Muslim League.

Formation of the All-India Muslim League 1906

  • The All-India Muslim League was formed in Dhaka in 1906, during the annual session of the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference.
  • Its aims were to inform the government of Muslim concerns and demands, to protect Muslim rights, and to improve relations between Muslims and the government while keeping friendly relations with other nations of the subcontinent.
  • The founding members included Sir Aga Khan, Nawab Viqar-ul-Mulk and Nawab Salimullah Khan. Sir Aga Khan was elected the first President of the Muslim League.

Minto-Morley Reforms 1909

  • The reforms, formally the Indian Councils Act of 1909, were named after Secretary of State John Morley and Viceroy Earl of Minto.
  • Their most important provision was separate electorates for Muslims — Muslims would elect their own representatives with their own votes.
  • Elected seats in the provincial councils and the Imperial Legislative Council were increased, but the British kept an official majority in the executive councils.

Annulment of the Partition of Bengal (1911)

  • Bengal was partitioned in 1905 on administrative grounds. The Hindu community opposed the partition and started the Swadeshi Movement, which boycotted British products and promoted indigenous goods.
  • On December 12, 1911, King George V declared the partition null and void. Muslims were disappointed and learned again that Congress was not interested in safeguarding Muslim interests.

Key Points

  • The Simla Deputation of 1906, with 35 members, demanded separate electorates from Lord Minto.
  • The Muslim League was founded at Dhaka in 1906, with Sir Aga Khan as its first President.
  • The Indian Councils Act 1909 granted separate electorates; the Bengal partition was annulled in 1911.

lessons.title: Lucknow Pact, Khilafat Movement and Jallianwala Bagh
lessons.notes_html:
Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was a great supporter of Hindu-Muslim unity, and the Lucknow Pact was the outcome of his vision. In December 1915, separate meetings of the Muslim League and the Congress were held in Bombay, and both parties set up committees to prepare a joint plan for amending the constitution.

Lucknow Pact 1916

  • In 1916, both parties met at Lucknow and approved a joint scheme of reforms.
  • Muslims were to be granted one-third of the seats in the Imperial Legislative Council, with a separate (independent) electorate.
  • Half the members of the Executive Council were to be elected by the Imperial Legislative Council, and provincial councils and provincial minorities were also considered.
  • By accepting separate electorates and one-third Muslim representation in the central council, the Congress accepted the Muslims as a separate nation for the first time.

Khilafat Movement 1919

  • The Indian Muslims held the Khilafat of the Ottoman Empire in the highest esteem. Turkey had allied with Germany in World War I, and after their defeat the Allied Forces decided, under the Istanbul Accord of November 3, 1918, to divide Turkey's territories among France, Greece and Britain.
  • The goals of the movement were: the Ottoman Khilafat must remain intact, Turkey's territorial unity must be preserved, and the holy places must not come under non-Muslim control.
  • Maulana Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Maulana Shaukat Ali played significant roles. Rallies and demonstrations were held, and a delegation of Muslim leaders went to England to raise the issue with the British parliament and prime minister.
  • During the movement, Hindu-Muslim unity was at its peak. Gandhi withdrew his support in early 1922 after his non-cooperation movement became violent, and the movement ended when Mustafa Kamal Ataturk abolished the Khilafat and declared the Republic of Turkey in March 1924.

Jallianwala Bagh Incident 1919

  • The Rowlatt Act of 1919 restricted civil liberties and allowed arrest and detention without trial, which caused protests all over India.
  • On April 13, 1919, on the Sikh festival of Baisakhi, thousands of people, including children, gathered at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, to oppose the Act and demand the release of detained political leaders.
  • General Reginald Dyer ordered his forces to lock the gates of the garden and open fire, killing hundreds of people in a short time.
  • The massacre was a turning point in India's struggle for independence and united diverse communities against colonial rule.

Key Points

  • Under the Lucknow Pact 1916, Congress accepted separate electorates and one-third Muslim seats at the centre.
  • The Khilafat Movement (1919-1924) defended the Ottoman Khilafat and showed peak Hindu-Muslim unity.
  • The Jallianwala Bagh massacre at Amritsar on April 13, 1919 strengthened the freedom struggle.

lessons.title: Simon Commission, Nehru Report and the Fourteen Points
lessons.notes_html:
Between 1920 and 1939, the struggle moved to constitutional demands. The British government appointed the Simon Commission in 1927 to propose constitutional reforms in India, as the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 had promised a commission within the next ten years.

Simon Commission 1927

  • The commission consisted of all British members — not a single Indian member was included.
  • Widespread protests and demonstrations started against this exclusion, and the uprising increased political consciousness among Indians, including Muslims, and strengthened the demand for constitutional reforms.
  • In response to the Simon Commission Report, the Congress later started the Civil Disobedience Movement.

Nehru Report (1928)

  • The Simon Commission faced strong opposition because it had no Indian member, so Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead challenged Indian leaders to prepare their own proposals for reforms.
  • A committee under Motilal Nehru prepared the Nehru Report, presented on August 28, 1928 at the Lucknow session of the all-party conference.
  • Its main points were: Dominion Status for India with a parliamentary form of government; no separate electorate for minorities; no reserved seats in Punjab and Bengal; an independent judiciary; one-fourth Muslim representation at the centre; and separation of Sindh from Bombay if it proved financially self-sufficient, with reforms in NWFP.
  • Muslim interests were not safeguarded and Muslim amendments were disregarded, so the Muslims rejected the report.

Fourteen Points of Quaid-e-Azam (1929)

  • In response to the Nehru Report, Quaid-e-Azam presented his Fourteen Points in 1929 at a session of the Muslim League. They were timely, moderate and authentic demands of the Muslim community.
  • They demanded a federal system with residuary powers in the provinces and equal provincial autonomy for all provinces.
  • They demanded separate electorates for Muslims, effective representation for minorities without reducing any majority to a minority, and one-third of seats reserved for Muslims in the central legislative assembly.
  • Other points included: Sindh as a separate province; reforms in Balochistan and NWFP; one-third Muslim ministers in central and provincial ministries; reserved seats for Muslims in government jobs; religious liberty for all communities; and constitutional protection for Muslim culture, education and language.
  • A bill concerning one religious community was not to be passed if three-fourths of that community's members opposed it, and constitutional amendments needed the approval of the provinces and states.

Key Points

  • The all-British Simon Commission of 1927 was boycotted across India.
  • The Nehru Report of 1928 ended separate electorates, so Muslims rejected it.
  • Jinnah's Fourteen Points of 1929 stated the minimum Muslim demands and became the League's charter.

lessons.title: Allahabad Address, Round Table Conferences and the 1935 Act
lessons.notes_html:
The Allahabad Address of 1930 gave the Pakistan Movement a clear destination. Allahabad hosted the 1930 annual session of the All-India Muslim League, presided over by Allama Muhammad Iqbal. It was the first time the notion of a separate Muslim homeland was presented.

Allahabad Address 1930

  • Iqbal said Islam is an all-encompassing moral framework that guides every part of society, unlike the West, where religion is treated as a private matter.
  • He strongly supported the Two-Nation Theory and opposed the idea of India as one united nation, arguing that Muslims and Hindus could not form a single nation.
  • He proposed that Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan be amalgamated into a single State, calling a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim State the final destiny of the Muslims, at least of North-West India.

Round Table Conferences 1930 to 1932

  • Indian parties were angry at the Simon Commission Report. Congress started the Civil Disobedience Movement, while Muslims demanded dialogue with all Indian communities, so the British government began constitutional negotiations.
  • London hosted three Round Table Conferences between 1930 and 1932. The first failed because the Congress leadership was absent; the second collapsed because Gandhi claimed to speak for the entire Indian population; Congress did not take part in the third.
  • The government's White Paper of 1933 contained the recommendations of these conferences, and the Government of India Act 1935 was based on them.

The Communal Award 1932

  • Separate electorates, first granted to Muslims by the Indian Councils Act 1909, had also been extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans, but the depressed classes had not received this right, and the issue stayed unresolved at the first two Round Table Conferences.
  • In 1932, the British government announced its own formula, the Communal Award, which ensured that Muslims and other minority groups kept their separate voting rights.
  • On the basis of weightage, Muslims gained greater representation in the Muslim-minority regions.

Government of India Act 1935

  • The British Parliament enacted the Act in 1935, keeping in view the Nehru Report, Quaid's Fourteen Points and the Round Table recommendations.
  • It increased provincial autonomy for India's 11 provinces, introduced a federal system of provinces and princely states, and divided powers through three lists — federal, provincial and concurrent.
  • Provincial legislatures were to be bicameral, a Federal Court was set up as the apex court, and separate electorates were retained for Muslims, Sikhs, Christians and others.
  • Many Indians were dissatisfied because the Viceroy and Governors kept wide powers. The central (federal) part was never implemented; only the provincial part was put into practice. The Act remained Pakistan's working constitutional arrangement until the first Constitution of 1956.

Key Points

  • Iqbal's Allahabad Address of 1930 first proposed a single Muslim state in the north-west.
  • Three Round Table Conferences (1930-1932) led to the White Paper of 1933 and the 1935 Act.
  • The Communal Award 1932 protected separate electorates; the 1935 Act gave provincial autonomy.

lessons.title: Congress Ministries, Lahore Resolution and Cripps Mission, 1937-1942
lessons.notes_html:
Under the Government of India Act 1935, elections for the provincial assemblies were held in 1937. The book records 1,785 seats in all, 102 of them allocated for Muslims. The Muslim League performed poorly, and the Congress formed ministries in eight of India's eleven provinces.

Congress Ministries 1937-1939

  • Muslims were under-represented in the Congress ministries, especially in key positions, and Muslim interests were ignored in governance.
  • The educational policies of the Congress ministries did not meet the religious and cultural needs of Muslims, raising fears for the protection of Muslim identity.
  • A worrying trend of assaults on Muslims developed in the provinces during Congress rule, and tensions between the communities increased.

Day of Deliverance

  • In November 1939, the Congress ministries resigned over their differences with the British about helping them in World War II.
  • On the appeal of Quaid-e-Azam, Muslims observed the Day of Deliverance (Youm-e-Nijat) on December 22, 1939, to mark the end of Congress rule.

Lahore Resolution 1940

  • The Lahore Resolution, also known as the Pakistan Resolution, was adopted at the Muslim League's annual session in Lahore's Minto Park (later Iqbal Park) in March 1940, presided over by Quaid-e-Azam.
  • Molvi Fazal-ul-Haq, the Chief Minister of Bengal, presented the resolution, and the session rejected the federation scheme of the 1935 Act as totally unsuited, unworkable and unacceptable to Muslim India.
  • The resolution stated that no constitutional plan would be acceptable to Muslims unless the Muslim-majority areas in the North-Western and Eastern Zones of India were grouped to form Independent States whose units would be autonomous and sovereign.
  • The word Pakistan was not used in the resolution, but it is widely known as the Pakistan Resolution. Pakistan Day is celebrated on 23 March every year to commemorate it.

Cripps Mission 1942

  • In March 1942, Sir Stafford Cripps of the British War Cabinet brought proposals to win Indian support for the war effort in World War II.
  • They offered a Constituent Assembly to frame a new constitution, dominion status for India, and the right for provinces unwilling to join the Indian dominion to form a separate state.
  • Both the Congress and the Muslim League rejected the proposals, as they did not satisfy their demands for complete autonomy and self-governance.

Quit India Movement

  • Mahatma Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement on August 8, 1942, at the Bombay session of the All-India Congress Committee, demanding that the British leave India at once.
  • The Muslim League disapproved of the movement. Instead of Quit India, Quaid-e-Azam demanded divide and quit India — the British should partition India and then withdraw, because Hindus would never do justice to Muslims in a united India.

Key Points

  • Congress ruled eight provinces from 1937 to 1939; Muslims marked its end as the Day of Deliverance on December 22, 1939.
  • The Lahore Resolution of March 1940 formally demanded independent Muslim states in the north-west and east.
  • The Cripps Proposals of 1942 were rejected by both Congress and the Muslim League.

lessons.title: From Simla Conference to Independence, 1945-1947
lessons.notes_html:
The political developments from 1940 to 1947 turned the demand of the Lahore Resolution into the reality of Pakistan.

Simla Conference (1945) and Elections 1945-46

  • Viceroy Lord Wavell called the Simla Conference in June 1945 to discuss postwar conditions in India. The Muslim League and Congress took part, but the conference failed because the two parties differed fundamentally over the composition of the future governing body.
  • In the elections of 1945-46, the Muslim League's manifesto was based on the Two-Nation Theory. In the central elections of December 1945, the League won all thirty Muslim reserved seats, and in the provincial elections it won about 90 percent of the Muslim seats.
  • This overwhelming victory proved that the Muslim League was the only representative party of the Muslims and that the majority of Muslims wanted a separate homeland, Pakistan.

The Cabinet Mission Plan 1946

  • Prime Minister Clement Attlee sent the Cabinet Mission to India in March 1946. Its three members were Lord Pethick-Lawrence, A. V. Alexander and Sir Stafford Cripps.
  • The plan, announced in May 1946, proposed a united federal Union of India, with the provinces grouped into Group A (Hindu-majority), Group B (Muslim-majority) and Group C (Bengal and Assam). The provinces would control all subjects except defence, foreign affairs and communications, and an interim government would work at the centre until a new constitution was framed.
  • The Muslim League rejected the plan because it did not protect Muslim interests and did not grant a separate Muslim state, and disagreement between Congress and the League caused the plan to fail.

June 3 Plan and the Independence Act 1947

  • Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy, advanced the transfer of power from June 1948 to August 1947. The plan, finalised in April 1947 and made public on June 3, 1947, divided British India into two dominions, India and Pakistan, each free to frame its own constitution.
  • The Sindh Assembly chose to join Pakistan; the Punjab and Bengal assemblies decided on partition; referendums in NWFP and Sylhet favoured Pakistan; and Balochistan's Shahi Jirga and Quetta Municipal Corporation decided to join Pakistan. The princely states could join either dominion.
  • The Indian Independence Act, approved on July 18, 1947, set up two independent Dominions, India and Pakistan, from August 15, 1947. Bengal and Punjab were partitioned, each Dominion's legislature received full law-making power, and the powers of the British Crown came to an end.
  • Under the Act, Pakistan came into being on August 14, 1947, and Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah became the first Governor-General of Pakistan.

Key Points

  • The Simla Conference of June 1945 failed over the shape of the future government.
  • The League's sweep of the 1945-46 elections — all 30 central Muslim seats — proved its mandate for Pakistan.
  • The June 3 Plan and the Independence Act 1947 created Pakistan on August 14, 1947.

lessons.title: Role of Political Leaders in the Making of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Political leaders, including women and minorities, played an important role in the Pakistan Movement.

Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah

  • Quaid-e-Azam, the most prominent leader of the Pakistan Movement, joined the All-India Muslim League in 1913, became its leader and made it a strong force for Muslim rights in British India.
  • He formulated and popularised the Two-Nation Theory — Hindus and Muslims as two separate nations — the ideological basis of the demand for a Muslim state.
  • He negotiated with the British, Congress and Sikh leaders for an orderly partition, became Pakistan's first Governor-General in August 1947, and helped solve the new state's early problems.

Allama Muhammad Iqbal

  • Allama Muhammad Iqbal, a philosopher, poet and politician, is regarded as an intellectual architect of the Pakistan Movement, the visionary who first proposed a distinct Muslim state.
  • In his Allahabad Address of 1930, he proposed a Muslim state in Muslim-majority north-western India — the framework for the later claim of Pakistan.

Liaquat Ali Khan and Choudhary Rahmat Ali

  • Liaquat Ali Khan, a leading Muslim League member and strong supporter of the Two-Nation Theory, helped formulate and pass the Pakistan Resolution in 1940; his diplomatic talents were vital in negotiations with the British. After independence he became Pakistan's first Prime Minister, guiding it through its formative years with economic and land reforms.
  • Choudhary Rahmat Ali, an architect of the Pakistan concept, published his leaflet Now or Never in 1933, stressing Muslim-Hindu differences. Dividing India into two states, he argued, was a practical long-term solution for peace — and he proposed the name Pakistan.

Role of Women in the Pakistan Movement

  • Fatima Jinnah, Quaid-e-Azam's sister, advanced her brother's ideology, became a political figure herself, and remained active in politics after his death. She is called Madar-e-Millat.
  • Begum Ra'ana Liaquat Ali Khan, wife of the first Prime Minister, championed women's rights, education and social welfare, and supported forming the All Pakistan Women's Association (APWA).
  • Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz, a Muslim League member, represented Muslim women's concerns before independence. Women leaders mobilised communities and campaigned for rights, education and social growth.

Role of Minorities in the Pakistan Movement

  • Jogendranath Mandal, a member of the All-India Scheduled Castes Federation and a notable Dalit leader, enthusiastically supported the Pakistan Movement and later became Pakistan's first Law Minister.
  • Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, another Dalit leader, supported the establishment of Pakistan as a means of ensuring Muslim political rights.
  • Satya Prakash Singha (S. P. Singha), born in Sialkot in 1893, supported the Lahore Resolution of 1940, was Speaker of the Punjab Assembly in united India, settled in Pakistan at independence, and died in 1948.

Key Points

  • Jinnah led the Muslim League and the Two-Nation Theory to the creation of Pakistan in 1947.
  • Iqbal proposed the separate Muslim state; Rahmat Ali named it Pakistan (1933).
  • Fatima Jinnah and Jogendranath Mandal led the women's and minorities' support.

lessons.title: Pakistan's Location and Extent
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan is located at the crossroads of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East. It is a land of diverse landscapes, extending from the towering peaks of the Karakoram and Hindu Kush ranges in the north to the vast plains of the Indus River Valley in the south, with lush forests, arid Balochistan deserts, meandering rivers and an enormous coastline.

Area and Extent

  • Pakistan is a South Asian country with a total area of 796,096 square kilometres (307,375 square miles).
  • It stretches 1,600 kilometres (994 miles) from north to south and 885 kilometres (550 miles) from east to west.
  • Geographically, Pakistan is located between latitudes 24° N and 37° N, and extends from longitude 61° East to 77° East.
  • Islamabad, the federal capital, is situated in the foothills of the Himalayas in the northern part of the country and is one of the most modern and well-planned capitals in the world.

Key Points

  • Pakistan stands at the crossroads of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East.
  • Its total area is 796,096 square kilometres; it stretches 1,600 km north-south and 885 km east-west.
  • Islamabad, in the Himalayan foothills, is the federal capital.

lessons.title: Geostrategic Importance of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's strategic location offers many opportunities to develop its economy and improve the lives of its people. By taking advantage of this location, Pakistan can become a major centre of trade and transportation, attracting foreign capital and driving economic expansion.

Advantages of Pakistan's Location

  • Transit trade: Pakistan provides a transit trade route to Afghanistan and the Central Asian states, which are landlocked countries with no access to the sea — and gains access to Central Asia's rich natural resources.
  • Access to global markets and energy resources: the Arabian Sea connects the Indian Ocean to the Persian Gulf, a major shipping route between South Asia, the Far East and the Middle East.
  • Increased trade with China: the rise of China has increased China-Pakistan trade; the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) is a major infrastructure project of the two countries.
  • Air routes: Pakistan lies at the intersection of two of the world's busiest air corridors — the North Atlantic and Asia-Pacific routes — making it a natural transit hub; Jinnah Terminal, Karachi is a significant international airport for passengers and cargo.
  • Abundant marine resources: the Arabian Sea is a vital waterway for global maritime trade, a source of oil and gas, and a habitat for fish, sharks and whales.
  • Tourism: from the ancient ruins of Mohenjo-Daro and Taxila to the Mughal-era architecture of Lahore and the Sufi shrines of Sindh, Pakistan's attractions draw visitors; new roads, railways and airports have increased tourist arrivals.

Using the Location Well

  • Pakistan can capitalise on its location by investing in infrastructure and transportation, improving trade relations with neighbours and promoting tourism.
  • Major challenges to its geostrategic importance are political instability, economic underdevelopment and lack of infrastructure.

Key Points

  • Pakistan's location gives it transit trade, sea and air routes, energy access and tourism potential.
  • CPEC links Pakistan with China's growing economy.
  • Political instability, underdevelopment and weak infrastructure are the main challenges.

lessons.title: Pakistan's Main Cities
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's major cities are home to a large segment of the population and contribute significantly to the economy. Urban centres are usually located near transportation hubs — motorways, airports and ports — which give easy access to markets at home and abroad. Pakistan's urban population is growing by about three percent per year; by 2030, more than half of the projected population of 250 million is expected to live in urban areas.

Cities of Punjab

  • Rawalpindi — part of the Islamabad-Rawalpindi metropolitan area and a major cantonment; population 2.098 million in 2017; a major transport hub with important commercial and wholesale markets and manufacturing and construction industries.
  • Lahore — the most populous city of Punjab and a significant cultural, historical, finance and trade hub; home to the Badshahi Mosque; a major centre for textile, food processing and engineering industries.
  • Faisalabad — a major agricultural and industrial hub, known as the Manchester of Pakistan for its thriving textile industry; also a major export centre and a region of rice and wheat cultivation.
  • Multan — a fertile agricultural region producing cotton, wheat, rice and sugarcane; an industrial centre with textile mills and food processing plants; known as the City of Saints for the shrines of Bahauddin Zakariya and Shah Rukn-e-Alam.

Cities of the North and West

  • Peshawar — capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in the north-west; a major transportation hub; the historic Khyber Pass trade route links Central and South Asia through it; monuments include Bala Hissar Fort and Mohabbat Khan Mosque.
  • Quetta — a major transportation hub connecting Balochistan with the rest of Pakistan and Afghanistan; known as the Fruit Garden of Pakistan for its pomegranates, apricots and apples; sights include Hanna Lake, the Ziarat Valley and Quetta Fort.
  • Gilgit-Baltistan — a region rich in hydroelectric potential (Diamer-Bhasha Dam), minerals, agricultural products and natural beauty, making tourism a valuable asset.
  • Karachi — the most populous city of Pakistan and its financial and commercial hub.

Key Points

  • Faisalabad is the Manchester of Pakistan; Multan is the City of Saints; Quetta is the Fruit Garden of Pakistan.
  • Lahore is Punjab's cultural and trade hub; Rawalpindi is a cantonment and transport hub.
  • Gilgit-Baltistan offers hydropower, minerals and tourism; Karachi is the financial hub.

lessons.title: The Northern and North-Western Mountains
lessons.notes_html:
Topography is the study of the Earth's surface features. Relief means the shape of the land — mountains, hills, valleys and passes. A mountain rises at least 2,000 feet (610 m); a mountain range is a chain of mountains of the same direction, age and formation; a hill is under 610 m. Pakistan's natural topography has six regions: the Northern and North-Western Mountains, the Western Mountains, the Balochistan Plateau, the Potwar Plateau and Salt Range, the Indus Plain, and the Desert Areas.

i. The Himalayas

  • The mighty Himalayas span about 2,500 kilometres from east to west and include the Deosai range, the Siwaliks, the Lesser Himalayas and the Central Himalayas.
  • The Siwaliks rise between 600 and 1,200 metres, the Lesser Himalayas from 1,800 to 4,500 metres and the Central Himalayas from 3,500 to 5,000 metres.
  • Important peaks include Everest, Nanga Parbat, Rakhiot, Ganalo and Sarwali; green coniferous forests and alpine meadows cover the region, which has great ecological significance and tourism potential.

ii. The Hindu Kush

  • The Hindu Kush extends from Afghanistan through Pakistan into Tajikistan, with an altitude of about 5,000 metres; its highest peak is Tirich Mir, 7,690 metres.
  • Vegetation is sparse in the cold climate, with alpine forests; above the snow line the mountains stay snow-capped all year, providing water for agriculture and hydropower.
  • Strategic passes — Shandur, Shangla and Lawarai — connect Gilgit, Chitral, Swat and Peshawar.
  • South of the Hindu Kush lie the sub-parallel Kohistan, Swat and Dir ranges, separated by rivers: Kohistan between the Indus and Swat, Swat between the Swat and Panjkora, and Dir between the Panjkora and Kunar; they fall from 5,000-6,000 metres in the north to 200 metres in the south.

iii. The Karakoram Mountains

  • The Karakoram spans 400 kilometres from the Hunza River to the Shyok River, north of the Indus, with an average elevation of 6,000 metres.
  • It holds the world's second-highest peak, K2 (Godwin-Austen or Chhogori), 8,611 metres.
  • The Khunjerab Pass links Pakistan to China through the Karakoram Highway, also known as the Silk Route.
  • Great glaciers — Siachen, Hispar, Baltoro and Batura — dominate the landscape; the Hunza, Gilgit and Nagar rivers drain the region, whose valleys (Skardu, Gilgit, Nagar) have low population density, with subsistence farming and pastoralism as the main livelihoods.

Key Points

  • The Himalayas, Hindu Kush and Karakoram form Pakistan's northern mountain wall.
  • K2 (8,611 m) in the Karakoram is the world's second-highest peak; Tirich Mir (7,690 m) tops the Hindu Kush.
  • The Khunjerab Pass connects Pakistan with China.

lessons.notes_html:
The Northern Mountains are a vital source of water and a shield for the whole country, but they are also a zone of natural disasters.

Importance

  • They are a massive reservoir of freshwater: snowmelt and glacial runoff feed the Indus River, which provides water for drinking, irrigation and hydropower to millions of people.
  • Their glaciers help regulate the climate and cool the planet.
  • They harbour unique and endangered wildlife, including the snow leopard and the Tibetan antelope.
  • They protect Pakistan from the cold winds of Siberia and Central Asia.
  • Economically they offer tourism (mountaineers and trekkers from around the globe), agriculture and forestry, and raw materials for the chemical, pharmaceutical, pulp and paper, and furniture industries.

Disasters in the Northern Mountains

  • An avalanche killed 14 people in the Northern Mountains in 2012, and another killed 20 people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2015.
  • A 7.6-magnitude earthquake killed over 73,000 people in Kashmir in 2005.
  • Floods killed over 1,700 people in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in 2010.
  • A landslide killed about 30 people in Gilgit-Baltistan in 2011.

Key Points

  • The northern mountains supply water, hydropower, wildlife habitat, tourism and protection from Siberian winds.
  • They are prone to avalanches, earthquakes, floods and landslides.
  • The 2005 Kashmir earthquake (7.6 magnitude, over 73,000 deaths) was the deadliest disaster listed.

lessons.title: The Western Mountains
lessons.notes_html:
The Western Mountains lie along Pakistan's western border and are lower than the Northern Mountains. They are divided into four main ranges.

i. Koh-e-Safed

  • Located south of the Kabul River, with the Kurram River flowing to their south, rising up to 4,700 metres; the highest peak is Sikaram, 4,760 metres.
  • Mostly snow-covered, they are called the White Mountains; they include the Khyber Pass, connecting Pakistan to Afghanistan, and have rugged topography, steep slopes and severe winters.

ii. Waziristan Hills

  • Located between the Kurram and Gomal rivers, with elevations up to 3,500 metres; the Tochi, Gomal and Kurram rivers join the Indus as its western tributaries, and the Tochi and Gomal are important passes; the Bannu valley lies here.
  • Key irrigation sources are the Kurram Tangi Dam on the Kurram River and the Gomal Zam Dam on the Gomal River.
  • The hills are rich in minerals, and their vegetation — oak, pine and juniper — is adapted to the harsh, arid climate.

iii. Suleiman Mountains

  • Situated west of the Indus River and south of the Waziristan Hills, they extend about 480 kilometres and merge into the Marri-Bugti hills in the south.
  • Their average height is 1,500 metres and the highest peak is Takht-e-Suleiman, 3,383 metres; the Bolan Pass connects Quetta and Sibbi.
  • They are composed of limestone, sandstone and shale rocks.

iv. Kirthar Ranges

  • Located south of the Bolan Pass, merging into the low hill ranges of Sindh, with an average height of 1,219 metres.
  • Gorakh Hill, at about 1,981 metres above sea level, is a famous hill station and tourist destination.

Economic Activities and Lifestyle

  • The western ranges have rugged terrain and sparse vegetation; most people live in small towns and rural areas with subsistence and nomadic lifestyles, and population density is below 100 people per square kilometre.
  • Canal irrigation is not feasible in most areas because of the terrain, so the Karez system is used for irrigation; roads, railways and air links are limited, and mineral extraction is hindered by the difficult terrain and maladministration.

Key Points

  • The four western ranges are Koh-e-Safed, Waziristan Hills, Suleiman Mountains and Kirthar Ranges.
  • The Khyber Pass (Koh-e-Safed) and Bolan Pass (Suleiman/Kirthar) are the great gateways of the west.
  • Life there is subsistence and nomadic, with Karez irrigation and sparse infrastructure.

lessons.title: The Balochistan Plateau
lessons.notes_html:
The Balochistan Plateau lies west of the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges, extending to Iran in the west, Afghanistan in the north and the Arabian Sea in the south. Its elevation ranges from about 600 to 300 metres and it covers a total area of 347,190 square kilometres. A basin is a large, generally level region enclosed by higher land, formed by the erosion of surrounding mountains and hills, with no outlet to the sea.

Basins and Ranges

  • Northern Basins: the Zhob and Loralai Basins, drained by the Zhob and Loralai rivers between the Toba Kakar and Sulaiman ranges; and the Quetta Valley, surrounded by mountain ranges south-west of the Loralai Basin.
  • Basins of Western Balochistan: inland drainage basins of salt lakes called Hamun — Hamun-e-Mashkel, Hamun-e-Murgho and Hamun-e-Lora — between the Chagai, Raskoh, Siahan and Central Makran ranges.
  • Toba Kakar Range: in the extreme north, rugged and without vegetation, rising above 3,000 metres and containing the Khojak Pass linking Pakistan with Afghanistan.
  • Chagai Hills (2,000 m) at the Pak-Afghan border; Raskoh Range (2,000 m) south of Chagai; the curved Siahan Range between Central Makran and Raskoh; Central Makran Range (1,000-1,200 m) in the south-west; and the Makran Coastal Range (200-600 m), the southernmost range along the coastal plain.
  • Kalat Plateau, south of Quetta, is crossed by the Kohi-Maran, Harboi, Brahui and Central Brahui ranges (1,600-2,000 m); the Khuzdar Knot south of it is a triangular region with many active faults and frequent earthquakes (1,800-2,400 m).

Economic Resources of Balochistan

  • Water: limited and unevenly distributed — surface water, groundwater (aquifers and springs) and the Karez system; over-extraction of groundwater is causing depletion.
  • Minerals: rich in gas, coal, copper, antimony and gold, but the sector is underdeveloped, contributing annual revenue of around Rs. 3.4 billion.
  • Fishing: the coastline has great potential — tuna, sardines and mackerels — but lacks port and processing infrastructure; the coastal highway and Gwadar port could revitalise it.
  • Agriculture: Balochistan is famous for fruit production, earning it the title Fruit Basket of Pakistan — almonds, apples, apricots, grapes, peaches, plums, pomegranates, cherries, dates and more.
  • Livestock: cattle, camels and poultry are kept for household milk and meat, and livestock products feed the leather, carpet and pharmaceutical industries.

Key Points

  • The Balochistan Plateau (347,190 sq km) holds basins, salt lakes (Hamuns) and dry ranges like Toba Kakar and Chagai.
  • It is rich in minerals and fruit but short of water.
  • The Khojak Pass links the plateau to Afghanistan.

lessons.title: The Potwar Plateau and Salt Range
lessons.notes_html:
The Potwar Plateau and Salt Range are situated south of Islamabad, lying between the River Indus and the River Jhelum, and span an area of approximately 26,000 square kilometres.

Physical Features

  • The Potwar Plateau is a highland with an average elevation of 500 to 1,000 metres above sea level, dissected by numerous streams and rivers, creating a badland topography.
  • The Salt Range runs from south-west to north-east; it is composed of sedimentary rocks, primarily sandstone and shale, and is famous for its extensive salt deposits.
  • Saline lakes — Kallar Kahar, Khabeki and Uchali — add to the scenic beauty of the region.
  • The Soan River drains the plateau; the Potwar Plateau is a rainfed (Barani) area.

Natural Resources and Economic Potential

  • Minerals: rich deposits of limestone, gypsum, marble, dolomite, coal and oil; oil and gas fields are set up in the area, such as the Attock Oil Refinery. These minerals serve construction, cement manufacturing and power generation.
  • Agriculture: water resources support agriculture through traditional irrigation methods; crops such as wheat and fruits are extensively cultivated.
  • Forestry: a source of timber and non-timber forest products, contributing to soil conservation and biodiversity preservation.
  • Tourism: scenic landscapes, historical sites and cultural attractions give the region potential to generate revenue and employment.

Key Points

  • The Potwar Plateau (500-1,000 m) lies between the Indus and Jhelum, south of Islamabad.
  • The Salt Range is famous for salt and also yields limestone, gypsum, coal and oil.
  • Kallar Kahar, Khabeki and Uchali are its saline lakes.

lessons.title: The Indus Plain and the Desert Areas
lessons.notes_html:
The Indus Plain is an extensive flat expanse formed by the River Indus and its tributaries, and it is the backbone of Pakistan's economy.

Tributaries of the Indus

Eastern TributariesWestern Tributaries
Jhelum RiverShyok River
Chenab RiverGilgit River
Ravi RiverKabul River
Sutlej RiverKurram River
Gomal River

The Upper Indus Plain

  • Covering the entire Punjab Province, it is nearly flat and slopes towards the south-west. Its natural features include:
  • Active flood plain: alongside the river, where the Indus deposits alluvium and meanders to form oxbow lakes, braided channels and levees.
  • Old flood plain: farther from the river, flooded periodically by heavy mountain rains; its alluvium makes it highly fertile and ideal for agriculture.
  • Piedmont plains: at the foothills of mountains, dominated by alluvial fans formed by streams from the Sulaiman, Kirthar and Siwalik mountains; agriculturally productive.
  • Doabs: the areas between rivers — Bari Doab (Lahore, Kasur, Okara, Sahiwal, Pakpattan, Vehari, Multan, Khanewal, Lodhran), Rechna Doab (Sialkot, Narowal, Gujranwala, Hafizabad, Jhang, Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh), Chaj Doab (Gujrat, Sargodha, Mandi Bahauddin, north-western Jhang) and Sindh Sagar Doab (Khushab, Mianwali, Leiah, Muzaffargarh).
  • Bar uplands: ancient interfluves in some doabs — Kirana Bar in Chaj Doab, Sandal Bar in Rechna Doab, Ganji Bar in Bari Doab and Nili Bar between the old beds of the Beas and Sutlej.

The Lower Indus Plain and Delta

  • In Sindh near Thatta, the Indus branches into distributaries that form a delta and join the sea at various points south-south-east of Karachi.
  • The delta covers an area of 3,000 square miles (7,800 sq km) or more and extends along the coast for about 130 miles (210 km).
  • Economic activities: fertile soil and a well-developed irrigation system make the plain ideal for agriculture; flat land and drainage suit settlement growth; mineral deposits and a developed transport network of air, railways and roads encourage industrialisation; main urban centres are Lahore, Sialkot, Faisalabad and Gujranwala.

The Desert Areas

  • Thal Desert: nestled between the Indus and Jhelum rivers (the Sindh Sagar Doab), with rolling sand dunes, hot summers and scant rainfall.
  • Thar Desert: in the south-east, comprising Cholistan (sandy plains, rocky outcrops, rich cultural heritage and wildlife), Nara (renowned for its unique flora) and Tharparkar (the largest of the three, across southern Sindh, with sand dunes and fertile agricultural pockets).
  • Kharan Desert: in south-western Balochistan, with rocky plateaus, gravel plains and scattered sand dunes supporting specially adapted flora and fauna.
  • Economic potential: deserts are rich in fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas; Cholistan holds lignite, gypsum and silica sand; Thar's coal deposits could generate electricity and its iron ore could produce steel. Canal water from Sukkur Barrage has transformed a major part of Thar into fertile farmland, and nomadic communities have traversed these lands for centuries.

Key Points

  • The Indus Plain divides into the Upper (Punjab) and Lower (Sindh) plains, ending in the Indus delta.
  • Doabs and bar uplands structure the Upper Indus Plain; flood plains make it fertile.
  • Thal, Thar (Cholistan, Nara, Tharparkar) and Kharan are Pakistan's deserts, rich in minerals and fuels.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Climate of Pakistan and Environmental Hazards

lessons.title: Climatic Zones of Pakistan: Highland and Lowland
lessons.notes_html:
Climate is the average of weather conditions over a long period, typically at least thirty years. Pakistan's overall climate is tropical or subtropical with semi-arid and arid conditions, but its varied topography creates four distinct climatic zones: Highland, Lowland, Desert (Arid) and Coastal (Maritime).

A. Highland Climate

  • It covers the northern, north-western and western mountainous regions — the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and Himalaya ranges.
  • It has distinct seasonal variations: prolonged, frigid winters and short, temperate summers.
  • Precipitation clearly increases with altitude: Muzaffarabad, Said-u-Sharif, Skardu, Astor, Dir, Parachinar and Kakul receive the highest rainfall in Pakistan, while Chitral and Gilgit get less rain because they lie in a rain-shadow area.
  • Lifestyle: cooler temperatures and abundant precipitation nurture forests and alpine meadows; people follow nomadic lifestyles and practise transhumance — the seasonal migration of livestock between high and low pastures. Subsistence agriculture, livestock herding and handiwork are the bedrock of livelihoods.
  • Climate change is hurting this zone: receding glaciers and declining water availability, deforestation reducing fodder, and floods and landslides damaging crops, irrigation systems, transport and communication.

B. Lowland Climate

  • It covers the plains of Punjab and Sindh (the Indus plain).
  • It has stark seasonal contrasts: arid, sometimes extreme summers and mild to cool winters.
  • Monsoon rains come from June to September; the lower Indus plain and southern regions receive much less rain, while the north and north-western parts catch the tail end of the monsoon. Most rain and thunderstorms occur in July and August.
  • The Potwar Plateau enjoys higher rainfall than the Indus plain because it has two rainfall sources — the monsoon and the western depressions.
  • Lifestyle: the Punjab plains are densely populated, with a well-developed canal irrigation system supporting crops like cotton, millet, wheat and sugarcane; heat waves, droughts and floods are the main climate threats.

Key Points

  • Pakistan has four climatic zones: Highland, Lowland, Desert (Arid) and Coastal.
  • Highland areas have long frigid winters, short cool summers and nomadic transhumance.
  • The lowland Indus plain has extreme summers, monsoon rain in July-August and canal irrigation.

lessons.title: Desert (Arid) and Coastal Climates
lessons.notes_html:
The arid zone covers the deserts and dry plateaus of Balochistan and Sindh, while the coastal zone runs along the Arabian Sea from the Rann of Kutch to the Makran coast.

C. Desert or Arid Climate

  • This zone has extremely low rainfall and a distinct seasonal contrast between hot summers and cool winters.
  • The Karez system — an underground irrigation system used in Balochistan for centuries — channels underground water to surface fields, allowing farmers to grow wheat, rice, millet and sorghum.
  • Livestock rearing is a crucial activity: sheep, goats and camels provide food, milk, wool and transportation.
  • The zone has a rich handicraft tradition — carpets, textiles, pottery, Ajrak, Ralli quilts, embroidered shawls and leather products — sold in local markets and exported.
  • Tourism is growing: the Cholistan Desert, with its sand dunes, salt marshes and ancient forts, attracts visitors for camel safaris and jeep tours.

D. Coastal or Maritime Climate

  • The coastal strip includes the Indus Delta, Thatta, Karachi and the whole Makran coast.
  • It has a maritime climate with sea breezes round the year and high humidity, particularly between April and September.
  • Very little rain falls in the monsoon season; some rainfall comes from the western depressions — in Sindh rain comes in the monsoon, while the Makran coast receives rain mainly in winter.
  • The sea moderates temperature: the temperature at Karachi is about 32 degrees in May, while June and October are the hottest months when dry, hot winds blow from the south-eastern desert across the coastal belt of Sindh.
  • Lifestyle: fishing is a cornerstone of the coastal economy; Karachi Fish Harbour is a major hub for processing and exporting seafood, and the Karachi-Korangi and Qasim ports are among the busiest in South Asia.
  • Climate change threatens this zone through rising sea levels, coastal erosion and more frequent, severe storms.

Key Points

  • The arid zone depends on the Karez system, livestock and handicrafts.
  • The coastal zone has sea breezes, high humidity, little rain and a fishing-based economy.
  • Karachi Fish Harbour and Port Qasim anchor the coastal trade.

lessons.title: Seasons, Temperature and Its Variations
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan has four distinct seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Temperature — the measure of hotness or coldness — is a central element of climate, shaping the ecological landscape and human activity.

The Seasons of Pakistan

  • Spring (March-May): temperatures rise gradually, ranging from 15°C to 25°C.
  • Summer (June-September): temperatures rise further to an average of 25°C to 40°C; the summer monsoon rains bring relief from the heat.
  • Autumn (October-November) and winter (December-February) complete the cycle, winter being cold in the north and mild in the south.

Temperature Across Pakistan

  • The northernmost region is the coldest: average summer temperature 17°C and winter temperature -2°C; the highest peaks are perpetually covered in snow.
  • Central Pakistan has a more temperate climate, with an average summer temperature of 25°C and winter temperature of 10°C.
  • Southern Pakistan is the hottest part of the country, with an average summer temperature of 28°C and average winter temperature of 18°C; this region includes Balochistan, a desert region, and Karachi, a port city.
  • According to the Pakistan Meteorological Department, the hottest months are May and June, with average temperatures of 30.5°C and 34.0°C respectively in the Karachi climate graph.
  • Karachi: the driest month is April with almost no rainfall; the highest rainfall occurs in July (about 52 mm).
  • Lahore: a local steppe climate with little rainfall; mean yearly temperature 24.0°C and about 636 mm of rain a year.

Factors Causing Temperature Variations

  • Angle of the sun: where the sun's rays fall vertically they deliver more heat; where they fall obliquely, less heat.
  • Latitudinal effect: at the equator the rays hit the Earth at a right angle; towards the poles they are oblique and spread out.
  • Altitude: air is dense at sea level and absorbs more heat; at higher altitude the air is thin and absorbs less, so temperature drops by about 6 degrees centigrade with every 1,000 feet increase in altitude.
  • Continental effect: land heats up and cools down more quickly than water; as distance from the sea increases, the continental effect increases and the effect of sea breezes decreases — strongest in arid regions like the Indus Valley and Balochistan Plateau.
  • Cloud cover decides how much sunlight reaches the surface and also affects precipitation and visibility.
  • Other factors: monsoon rains, distance from the sea and sea breezes.

Key Points

  • Pakistan has four seasons; May and June are the hottest months.
  • The north is coldest, the centre temperate and the south hottest.
  • Temperature varies with the sun's angle, latitude, altitude, cloud cover and distance from the sea.

lessons.title: Sources of Rainfall in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Rainfall decreases from the Himalayas towards the south of Pakistan. Pakistan's rain comes from several distinct sources, the most important being the monsoon.

i. Monsoon Winds

  • The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season, because these seasonal winds change their course twice a year.
  • Monsoon rainfall normally lasts from June to September and comes from two branches — the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
  • Bay of Bengal branch: in summer the land heats up faster than the sea, a low-pressure area develops over the land, and warm, moist air rushes in from the Bay of Bengal, crosses India, hits the Himalayas and gives rain to the northern areas of KPK and Punjab.
  • Arabian Sea branch: active monsoon winds blow across the south-east of Pakistan and bring rain to the coastal areas; they recharge groundwater and supply water for agriculture, but can also cause landslides and flooding.
  • Pressure and the monsoon: in summer the sea becomes a low-pressure area compared with the land, so moisture-laden winds flow from sea to land and bring rain over northern and central Pakistan; in winter the gradient reverses, winds blow from land to sea, and rainfall is minimal.

ii. Western Depressions

  • Western depressions (western disturbances) are low-pressure systems that develop over the Mediterranean Sea and travel eastward, bringing rain and snow to the Middle East and South Asia.
  • They affect Pakistan's northern and western regions — Chitral, Dir, Peshawar, Loralai, Quetta, Kharan and the Makran coastal range — and are most common from November to March.
  • Their winter precipitation and snowfall are very beneficial for agriculture: the snow melts in summer and supplies irrigation water.

iii. Convectional Currents

  • Heated land warms the air above it; the warm air rises rapidly to the condensation level, cools, condenses and forms clouds that give rain.
  • Convectional rainfall occurs in northern Punjab and KPK (Rawalpindi, Peshawar) in early summer.
  • It does not occur in the south because of the temperature inversion layer, which forces rising air back down, traps pollutants and creates dryness and heat — which is why Karachi and adjoining areas receive no convectional rainfall in summer despite temperatures around 40°C.

iv. Relief Rainfall

  • Moist air forced to ascend over mountains expands and cools; at the condensation level the vapour condenses into clouds and falls as rain, while dry air descends on the leeward side (the rain shadow).
  • It is common in the Himalayas and Karakoram, which block the moisture-bearing winds from the Bay of Bengal; important places include Murree, Abbottabad, Swat Valley, Gilgit-Baltistan, Peshawar, Kohat, Bannu and Quetta.

v. Tropical Cyclones

  • Tropical cyclones — called hurricanes or typhoons in other regions — are massive rotating storms that originate over warm ocean waters, with strong winds, torrential rainfall and destructive storm surges.
  • Pakistan's coastal areas of Sindh and Balochistan face these storms; Karachi, Thatta, Badin, Pasni, Jiwani and Gwadar face the highest risk.

Key Points

  • Pakistan's rainfall sources are the monsoon, western depressions, convectional currents, relief rainfall and tropical cyclones.
  • The monsoon (June-September) blows from sea to land in summer and land to sea in winter.
  • Western depressions bring winter rain and snow from November to March.

lessons.title: Rainfall and Farming
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's rainfall comes mainly from the monsoon in summer and western depressions in winter. Because its timing, amount and distribution vary, its effectiveness for agriculture is limited, and farming depends largely on the irrigation system, which is fairly developed in Punjab and Sindh.

How Effective is the Rainfall?

  • Monsoon rainfall is most effective in the northern and central parts, where it is more abundant and evenly distributed.
  • Parts of the Potwar Plateau have canal irrigation; the remaining parts are Barani lands — areas dependent on rain — where badland topography stops rainwater being absorbed or used effectively.
  • In the south, monsoon rainfall is more variable and less reliable.
  • Torrential monsoon rain is not effective: the land cannot absorb it and it causes floods; reservoirs and dams on the Indus store the extra water for irrigation.

Winter Rainfall: Advantages and Disadvantages

Replenishes groundwater aquifers, dams and reservoirs for the dry summerLate winter rain delays sowing of spring crops like cotton and sugarcane
Supports rabi crops such as wheat, barley and lentilsHeavy rain causes soil erosion on sloping lands

Key Points

  • Rainfall is unreliable in timing and distribution, so farming depends on irrigation.
  • Barani lands depend on rain alone, mainly in the Potwar Plateau and southern Punjab.
  • Winter rain helps rabi crops and water storage but can flood fields and delay sowing.

lessons.title: Environmental Hazards: Thunderstorms and River Floods
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan faces several environmental hazards linked to its climate, including thunderstorms, river floods and droughts.

i. Thunderstorms

  • Thunderstorms are most common in the summer months of April to June and September to October.
  • They are most common in the north and north-western areas and the foothills of the Himalayas and Safed Koh mountains.
  • They bring strong winds, heavy rain, lightning, thunder and hail, which can destroy crops and orchards and cause flooding, landslides and power outages.

ii. River Floods

  • A river flood occurs when a river overflows its banks and inundates the surrounding land. Floods also bring benefits: they deposit fresh nutrients and a layer of alluvium in wetlands and the Indus delta and recharge groundwater.
Natural FactorsHuman Factors
Record-breaking or torrential rainfallDeforestation, which reduces infiltration and increases surface run-off
Fast melting of snow due to climate changeBuilding settlements on the floodplains
Riverbanks too low to hold the floodwaterReduced capacity of dams to store extra flood water
Sea storms raising sea level in coastal areasFlood authorities unprepared for major rainfall events

Government Measures to Prevent Floods

  • Early warning systems so farmers can evacuate animals, sandbag and harvest early.
  • Promoting flood insurance for financial recovery from flood losses.
  • Forest conservation — afforestation and reafforestation to regulate water flow.
  • Urban planning to limit impervious surfaces that hinder water infiltration.
  • Flood-resilient infrastructure, improved drainage systems and flood defence structures such as levees and floodwalls.
  • Water resource management — small dams to control water flow — plus flood awareness, education and rehabilitation centres for victims.

Key Points

  • Thunderstorms strike mainly in April-June and September-October in the north.
  • Floods have natural causes (torrential rain, snowmelt) and human causes (deforestation, floodplain settlements).
  • Early warnings, insurance, forests, levees and small dams are the main government defences.

lessons.title: Droughts and Drought Management
lessons.notes_html:
A drought is a long period of abnormally low rainfall leading to a shortage of water. Pakistan faces both natural and human-induced droughts, in several common forms.

Forms of Drought

  • Permanent drought: exists in the desert areas of Pakistan, particularly the deserts of Balochistan and Thar, with extremely low precipitation and limited water; crop cultivation is very challenging, and communities adapt through subsistence farming and livestock rearing.
  • Seasonal drought: the Barani regions — the Potwar Plateau and parts of southern Punjab — are prone to seasonal droughts because of the unreliable nature of rainfall.
  • Invisible drought (agricultural drought): a subtle threat often triggered by human factors such as deforestation and excessive soil erosion, which reduce soil moisture and water infiltration, so crop yields and livestock productivity fall.
  • Unpredictable drought: characterised by erratic rainfall patterns and reduced precipitation, often attributed to climate change; it causes crop failures and water scarcity and is hard to plan against.

Drought Management in Pakistan

  • Water conservation schemes to conserve water resources before time.
  • Early warning systems and financial aid for the people affected by droughts.
  • Drought-resistant crops and drip irrigation: promote crops like sorghum and millet and water-efficient drip irrigation (genetically modified crops must be examined for health effects).
  • Community-based drought management so communities can store and share resources through dry seasons.

Key Points

  • Droughts in Pakistan are permanent, seasonal, invisible and unpredictable.
  • Permanent drought rules the Thar and Balochistan deserts; seasonal drought hits the Barani areas.
  • Water conservation, early warnings, resistant crops and drip irrigation are the main responses.

lessons.title: Surface Water Resources: The Indus River System
lessons.notes_html:
Water resources are indispensable for human life, ecosystems, agriculture, industry and energy. Our bodies contain roughly 60% water, and no life can survive without a consistent supply of clean water. Pakistan has many surface and groundwater resources that meet its domestic, industrial and agricultural needs.

The Indus River System

  • The Indus is Pakistan's longest river, flowing from Tibet through India into Pakistan, and provides the majority of the country's surface water.
  • It is joined by important tributaries — the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej — to form the vast Indus River System.

Dams and Barrages

  • Tarbela Dam, on the Indus River, is one of the world's largest earth-filled dams; it stores water for agriculture, generates hydropower and controls floods.
  • Mangla Dam, on the Jhelum River, is another large reservoir supplying water for irrigation, hydropower generation and flood control.
  • Chashma Barrage, on the Indus in Mianwali District of Punjab, regulates agricultural water flow and supports management of the Indus River System.

Canals

  • Pakistan has a vast network of canals channelling water from the Indus and its tributaries to agricultural fields, including the Upper Bari Doab Canal and Lower Bari Doab Canal in Punjab and the Rohri Canal and Nara Canal in Sindh.
  • The Indus Basin Irrigation System is the world's largest irrigation network, serving 14.4 million hectares of cultivated land.

Key Points

  • The Indus and its tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej) supply most of Pakistan's surface water.
  • Tarbela (Indus) and Mangla (Jhelum) are the great storage dams; Chashma is a major barrage.
  • Pakistan's canal irrigation network is the largest in the world, serving 14.4 million hectares.

lessons.title: Groundwater Resources and Seasonal Fluctuations
lessons.notes_html:
Groundwater is stored in aquifers — underground geological structures that hold and convey water. Pakistan's groundwater is critical for sustaining agriculture, providing drinking water and supporting economic activities.

The Aquifer Systems

  • Indus Basin Aquifer: the Indus Basin Irrigation System is the world's biggest contiguous surface water irrigation system, and its canals also form a gigantic reservoir of groundwater beneath the plains of Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
  • Balochistan Basin Aquifer: covers around 25% of Pakistan's total land area in various sub-basins; in western Balochistan, where surface water is sparse and unpredictable, it is the primary supply of groundwater for home and agricultural use.
  • Kirthar Fold Belt Aquifer: located near the western boundary of the Indus Basin; it provides groundwater in sections of Sindh and Balochistan, where its water quality is generally superior to that of the Indus Basin Aquifer.

Seasonal Fluctuations in Flow and Quality

  • Summer monsoon (July-September): heavy rain causes a large rise in river flow, especially in the upper Indus and its tributaries; flooding can occur, and floodwater carries toxins from urban and agricultural areas, degrading water quality.
  • Winter (November-February): river flow drops because low temperatures slow the melting of snow in the northern mountains; this low-flow period corresponds with the Rabi season, when crops such as wheat are cultivated.
  • Spring (March-May): as temperatures rise, snowmelt gradually increases the flow, helping farmers prepare for planting and early cultivation.

Key Points

  • Groundwater sits in aquifers: the Indus Basin, Balochistan Basin (25% of the land) and Kirthar Fold Belt systems.
  • River flow peaks in the monsoon (July-September) and falls in winter (November-February).
  • Monsoon floods raise flow but lower water quality; spring snowmelt restarts the flow.

lessons.title: The Irrigation System: Advantages and Disadvantages
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's irrigation system is built on a vast network of canals emanating from the Indus River and its major tributaries. It is the backbone of the agricultural economy, but it has both advantages and disadvantages.

Advantages

  • It supports a wide variety of crops — rice, wheat, sugarcane and cotton — and, by supplying water in both Kharif and Rabi seasons, allows year-round cultivation and multiple cropping, increasing agricultural yield.
  • It provides a consistent and controlled supply of water, decreasing farmers' reliance on uncertain rainfall and lowering the risks of drought and inconsistent weather.
  • Crop diversity under irrigation contributes to food security and economic stability.
  • Large reservoirs and barrages, like Tarbela Dam, Mangla Dam and Sukkur Barrage, generate hydropower, meeting energy needs while reducing dependency on fossil fuels.
  • Reservoirs store water and regulate flow during the monsoon season of excess water, and barrages and canals are designed to reduce the impact of floods.

Disadvantages

  • Salinity: irrigation-induced salinity is a serious problem — excessive salts build up in the soil over time, lowering fertility and production (with waterlogging).
  • Conveyance losses: inefficiencies in canals and distributaries cause significant water losses during transport.
  • Maintenance: old canals and barrages need frequent maintenance and updates; inadequate investment decreases the system's efficacy.
  • Unjust distribution: regional differences in water availability mean some regions have more consistent access than others.
  • Climate change alters precipitation patterns, changing the timing and availability of water supplies.

Key Points

  • Irrigation gives year-round cropping, food security, hydropower and flood regulation.
  • Its main problems are salinity and waterlogging, conveyance losses, poor maintenance and unequal distribution.
  • Climate change is making water supply less predictable.
