lessons.title: Sustainable Solutions to Water Resources Management
lessons.notes_html:
To deal with the threatening issues of water pollution, water shortage and wastage, Pakistan needs a comprehensive, long-term strategy that balances the needs of agriculture, industry and home consumers with environmental conservation.

The Sustainable Solutions

  • Encourage modern irrigation techniques such as drip irrigation and sprinkler systems, which reduce water waste and improve efficiency; encourage rainwater harvesting and soil moisture monitoring.
  • Give farmers and enterprises incentives to improve groundwater recharge, such as avoiding excessive pumping during critical periods.
  • Implement large-scale afforestation programmes to preserve watersheds, minimise soil erosion and improve the soil's natural water retention.
  • Promote soil conservation practices to reduce runoff and sedimentation, protecting water quality in rivers and reservoirs.
  • Invest in wastewater treatment plants to handle sewage and industrial effluents before they are discharged into water bodies.
  • Invest in canal system repair and modernisation to reduce conveyance losses and prevent waterlogging, using sensor networks, real-time monitoring and automated control systems.
  • Encourage rainwater harvesting devices in metropolitan areas to store rainwater for non-potable uses, reducing demand on traditional supplies.
  • Encourage crops that are well-suited to the existing water resources and climate, and provide farmers with education and extension services on irrigation scheduling.
  • Build climate-resilient water infrastructure for shifting precipitation patterns and temperature swings.
  • Run public awareness campaigns to increase water literacy and promote responsible water use at individual and community levels.

Key Points

  • Drip and sprinkler irrigation, rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge save water.
  • Afforestation, soil conservation and wastewater treatment protect water quality.
  • Modernised canals, suitable crops and public awareness complete the strategy.

lessons.title: Role of Dams, Barrages, Canals and Reservoirs
lessons.notes_html:
Dams, barrages, canals and water reservoirs tackle many water-related concerns in Pakistan — hydroelectric power generation, flood control and irrigation — though they also influence agriculture, the environment, industry and human activities.

What Each Structure Does

  • Dams store water during high-flow periods such as the monsoon, ensuring a supply for dry times; they generate hydropower — a renewable, clean source of energy — and regulate river flow, reducing the impact of floods.
  • Barrages are built across rivers to control the flow of water: they regulate flow into downstream areas, reduce flooding, guarantee consistent water availability and manage the diversion of water into the canal network at canal headworks. Sukkur, Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu and Kotri barrages are critical components of Pakistan's irrigation infrastructure.
  • Canals distribute water from rivers and reservoirs to fields for large-scale irrigation and controlled allocation: main canals take water straight from rivers or reservoirs, branch canals branch off to specific areas, and distributaries deliver water directly to the fields; well-designed canals with suitable drainage also reduce waterlogging.

Impacts

  • On agriculture: canals and barrages give a stable water supply all year, allowing several cropping seasons and greater productivity; reservoirs store surplus water for dry seasons — but poor drainage practices cause waterlogging and salinity, and dams trap sediments, diminishing the fertility of agricultural land downstream.
  • On the environment: hydropower is clean energy that lowers dependency on fossil fuels — but dams change natural river flow patterns, affecting downstream ecosystems, sediment transport, nutrient cycling and biodiversity.
  • On industry: dams contribute considerably to hydropower, a cheap and renewable energy source for industrial activity, and provide water for industrial processes — but industry in flood-prone locations downstream is vulnerable during high flows, and industrial discharges into canals and rivers damage water quality.
  • On human activities: reservoirs support fishing and recreation and secure drinking water, while large projects can displace people and change community life along the rivers.

Key Points

  • Dams store water and make hydropower; barrages control and divert river flow; canals distribute it.
  • Sukkur, Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu and Kotri are the key barrages.
  • Benefits come with costs: waterlogging, salinity, sediment trapping and changed river ecosystems.

lessons.title: Population Growth, Density and the Census
lessons.notes_html:
The population growth of a country is linked to its birth rate and death rate, and to migration, which changes the composition and distribution of population. Pakistan is the 5th largest country in the world by population, after China, India, USA and Indonesia.

Rate of Natural Increase

  • The rate of natural increase is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate: Rate of Natural Increase = Birth Rate − Death Rate.
  • For more than five decades the death rate has declined because of better sanitation, medical facilities and potable water, and diseases like cholera, malaria and typhoid have been brought under control.
  • In 2020, the rate of natural increase for Pakistan was 20.54 persons per thousand population.

Population and Density

  • Pakistan's population grew from 32.7 million in 1947 to 207.68 million in the 2017 census, with a density of 260.88 people per square kilometre.
  • The estimated population was 229.22 million in 2022 (density 287.93 per sq km), and in 2023 the total population was projected to be 241.49 million (Pakistan Bureau of Statistics).
  • In the 2017 census the rural population was 132.01 million and the urban population 75.67 million; by 2022 the urban population had risen to 84.69 million, and the urban share reached 38.82% in 2023.

The Population Census

  • A census is the complete count of the population of a nation or region; it records characteristics such as age, sex and occupation, and may include data on agriculture and business. National governments usually conduct censuses every five to ten years, as recommended by the United Nations.
  • Importance: the census provides an economic frame to determine the size of economic clusters across the country; it helps governments distribute funds and assistance to provinces, districts and localities; it is used for the reappropriation of National Assembly seats by drawing legislative districts; and its data serves research, marketing and planning — for example, where schools are constructed or new bus routes placed.

Key Points

  • Natural increase = birth rate − death rate; it was 20.54 per thousand in 2020.
  • Population rose from 32.7 million (1947) to 207.68 million (2017), density 260.88 per sq km.
  • The census guides funds, National Assembly seats and development planning.

lessons.title: The Demographic Transition Model
lessons.notes_html:
The Demographic Transition Model is a predictable five-stage model that explains population growth patterns as a country develops.

The Five Stages

StageBirth RateDeath RateNatural Increase
1HighHighStable or slow increase
2HighFalls rapidlyVery rapid increase
3FallingFalls more slowlyIncrease slows down
4LowLowStable or slow increase
5Very lowLowStable or slow decrease

Pakistan Through the Stages

  • Stage 1 (Pre-Industrial): both birth and death rates are high, so growth is slow; Pakistan's historical birth rate averaged around 40 births per 1,000 people, with poor healthcare and sanitation.
  • Stage 2 (Transition): improved medical facilities, sanitation and food production cut the death rate — Pakistan's death rate fell from 27 per 1,000 in the 1950s to 7 per 1,000 in the 2020s — while birth rates stayed high; cities like Karachi, Lahore and Faisalabad led the mortality decline.
  • Stage 3 (Modern Society): improving economic conditions, education and family-planning awareness bring the birth rate down; women are more career-oriented and marry late, and education plays a significant role in reducing fertility.
  • Stage 4 (Post-Industrial): Pakistan is yet to reach Stage 4, with its low and stable birth and death rates; its population growth rate is still around 1.9%, so continued efforts in education, healthcare and family planning are crucial.
  • Stage 5 (Late Post-Industrial): Pakistan's population is projected to keep growing, reaching 280 million by 2030; sustained economic growth, improved healthcare and changing social norms will shape its future trajectory.

Key Points

  • The model has five stages, from high birth and death rates to very low birth rates.
  • Pakistan has passed through Stages 1-3 and has not yet reached Stage 4.
  • Its death rate fell from 27 to 7 per 1,000 between the 1950s and the 2020s.

lessons.notes_html:
Population structure is the overall composition of a country's population. Pakistan's structure is shown by its population pyramid (2022).

Reading Pakistan's Pyramid

  • The pyramid has a wide base in the 0-14 years age group, which means the population is youthful, with high fertility trends and a large dependent group as a result.
  • There is a proportional decrease in the ratio of population for the 15 to 65 years age group and beyond.
  • Nearly 35% of the population is under the age of 15 — a result of high birth rates and a decline in infant mortality.

Opportunity and Challenge

  • A youthful population offers potential economic benefits in terms of a vast pool of manpower in the future.
  • But it also presents challenges regarding resource allocation, infrastructure development and social stability, because a large share of the population depends on the working-age group.

Key Points

  • Pakistan's pyramid has a wide base: about 35% of people are under 15.
  • A large dependent group burdens the working-age population.
  • The youth bulge is both future manpower and a present planning challenge.

lessons.title: Reasons for High Population Growth
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's population grows rapidly for social, cultural and economic reasons rooted in its rural life.

The Main Reasons

  • Children as farm labour: subsistence farming has fostered a cultural preference for large families, because children are seen as additional labour on the farm, reducing reliance on hired labour — though this ignores long-term challenges like resource scarcity and reduced access to education.
  • Early marriages are deeply entrenched in rural traditions and further the growth trend.
  • Preference for sons: sons are often perceived as a source of economic support, weakening the message of gender equality.
  • Weak family planning: awareness of family planning's benefits for maternal health is low; poverty is a barrier to education, which perpetuates the poverty cycle and limits access to family-planning information; and frequent changes in government policies have undermined family-planning programmes.
  • Afghan refugees: the influx of Afghan refugees has also contributed to population growth and placed additional strain on resources and infrastructure.

The Urban-Rural Divide

  • Rural life is simple and rustic, with close-knit communities, villages surrounded by agricultural land, an economy based on agriculture, livestock and natural resources, sparse population, strong community ties, limited social mobility and limited access to modern technology.
  • Urban life is complex and fast-paced, with cities of dense buildings and infrastructure, an economy of trade, commerce, industry and services, dense and diverse population, greater social mobility, specialised labour and greater access to technology, communication, transport and healthcare.

Key Points

  • Large-family preference, early marriage and son preference drive high growth.
  • Poverty, low education and unstable family-planning policies sustain it.
  • Rural and urban Pakistan differ sharply in lifestyle, economy and opportunities.

lessons.title: Population Distribution and Density Factors
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan's population density shows significant spatial variations, shaped by natural and human factors. Balochistan is the most scarcely populated province, while the Indus plains are densely settled.

Natural Determinants

  • Rugged terrain and extreme climate: the northern highlands — Karakoram, Himalayas and Hindu Kush — have frigid temperatures, heavy snowfall and frequent landslides, making them less habitable, with lower densities in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
  • Arid landscapes and limited resources: south-western Balochistan, including the Kharan Desert, faces severe water scarcity and limited agricultural potential; Kohat, Bannu and the Waziristan Hills have rugged terrain, low rainfall and poor transport links that hinder population growth.
  • Fertile plains and abundant resources: Punjab and Sindh have higher densities because fertile plains, moderate rainfall and reliable water from the Indus and its tributaries, lakes and canals support agriculture and attract population.

Human Factors

  • Urbanisation and economic opportunities: the availability of resources and jobs in cities strongly influences density — Karachi has a population density of over 1,500 people per square kilometre, and Lahore and Faisalabad have densities of 1,000-1,500 per square kilometre.
  • Infrastructure and amenities: major cities offer superior transport networks, power, housing schemes, education, healthcare and recreational facilities, attracting a large influx of people seeking better employment and a higher quality of life.

Key Points

  • Density is low in the rugged, arid north and west and high in the fertile Indus plains.
  • Karachi exceeds 1,500 people per sq km; Lahore and Faisalabad reach 1,000-1,500.
  • Water, fertile land, jobs and amenities pull people; terrain and aridity push them away.

lessons.title: Migration: Rural-Urban and Seasonal
lessons.notes_html:
Migration is the movement of people from one place to another. Pakistan's demographic landscape is characterised by rural-to-urban migration, which has intensified since independence.

Push and Pull Factors

Push Factors (rural)Pull Factors (urban)
Poverty and low wagesDemand for labour and high wages
High unemployment and over-populationStrong economic growth
Poor health careGood healthcare and education systems
Natural disasters and famineFamily and friends / networks
Discrimination, corruption, crimeRights and freedoms, law and order, amenities
  • Urban areas, with their infrastructure, education, healthcare, sanitation, housing, recreation and employment, exert a powerful pull effect; limited development, scarce amenities and lack of jobs in rural areas push people towards cities.

Seasonal Migration in Rural Areas

  • Transhumance: in the northern mountains, extreme winters make living difficult, so communities move with their livestock to lower-lying areas in winter and return to the highland pastures in spring when the snow melts.
  • Nomadism: prevalent in the arid regions — the Thal, Kharan and Cholistan deserts — where scarcity of water and vegetation drives continuous movement with herds of sheep, goats, camels and donkeys, which provide food, milk and income.
  • Harvesting-season migration: people who migrated to urban centres for employment return to their villages during the harvesting season to help with labour-intensive tasks; cotton picking and sugarcane harvesting are prime examples.

Key Points

  • Rural-urban migration is driven by push factors at home and pull factors in cities.
  • Seasonal migration takes three forms: transhumance, nomadism and harvesting-season returns.
  • Transhumance follows the seasons in the mountains; nomadism follows water in the deserts.

lessons.title: Urbanisation: Problems, Solutions and Brain Drain
lessons.notes_html:
Urbanisation means town or city life — areas of large, dense population whose main occupations are in secondary industries and tertiary activities such as services, trade and commerce. Lahore is the capital of Punjab and its largest urban centre; Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar show both the promise and the problems of urban growth.

Problems Caused by Urbanisation

  • Lack of accommodation: newcomers live in slums or kachi abadis with poor living standards and many hazards.
  • Environmental issues: untreated domestic and industrial waste causes water and land pollution and health hazards; large numbers of vehicles cause air pollution, carbon emissions, traffic jams and frequent accidents.
  • Depletion of resources: migrants settle in unplanned houses on city outskirts with shortages of education, health, transport and electricity, which also leads to unemployment.
  • Psychological problems and crime: crime increases due to unemployment and the mixing of people; depression and drug abuse grow, and the great economic gap between the 'haves' and 'have-nots' also leads to crime.

Solutions for Urbanisation

  • Improve transport with metalled roads, overhead bridges and underpasses, and introduce public transport to reduce vehicles on the road.
  • Spread awareness on using electricity, gas and water sustainably; increase the number of tax filers so more funds are available for development.
  • Build facilities to treat industrial and domestic waste.
  • Control rural depopulation by providing quality education, electricity, safe drinking water and small-scale industries in rural areas.
  • Develop better-quality, affordable and subsidised housing schemes through the public and private sectors.

Brain Drain and Sustainable Growth

  • From 1971 to 2022, a total of 6,019,888 highly qualified and skilled professionals migrated from Pakistan: 251,677 (4.18%) highly qualified, 455,097 (7.55%) highly skilled and 5,314,004 (88.27%) skilled professionals — a serious brain drain.
  • Strategies for sustainable population growth include agricultural development in the rural sector, adult education programmes, expanding market access for Pakistani goods, supporting SMEs in export activities and promoting brand awareness and marketing — ensuring food security, economic development and enhanced living standards.

Key Points

  • Urbanisation brings slums, pollution, resource depletion, unemployment and crime.
  • Solutions: public transport, waste treatment, rural development and affordable housing.
  • Brain drain took over 6 million skilled people abroad between 1971 and 2022.

lessons.title: Agriculture as a System
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan is an agrarian country, and agriculture is the backbone of food production for its growing population. Agriculture means cultivating land for crop production and rearing livestock; it is a primary sector activity. Agriculture contributes 19.2% to GDP and employs 38.5% of the labour force; over 65% of the population depends on it for their livelihood.

Inputs, Processes and Outputs

InputsProcessesOutputs
Natural/physical: land, water, air, sunlight, soil, mineralsPlanting, weeding, irrigating, threshing, harvestingCrops and non-food products: cotton, wheat, rice, vegetables, fruits, flowers, wool, biofuels
Human: labour, capital, machinery, seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, waterFeeding, breeding, caring for animals, milkingLivestock and dairy products: milk, meat, eggs
  • Natural inputs provide the base: land for crops and livestock, water for growth, and climate — the interplay of temperature, precipitation and sunlight — which decides which crops and livestock suit an area.
  • Human inputs include skills and labour, and capital, which buys machinery such as tractors and harvesters, fertilizers, equipment and infrastructure for efficient, large-scale production.
  • Technology introduces innovations such as GM crop varieties, improved livestock breeds and good farming practices, improving productivity and resilience.
  • Profit is invested back into the farm for new investment, equipment, land or livestock.

Key Points

  • Agriculture is a system of inputs, processes and outputs.
  • It contributes 19.2% of GDP and employs 38.5% of the labour force.
  • Natural inputs are land, water and climate; human inputs are labour, capital and technology.

lessons.title: Types of Farming and Cropping Seasons
lessons.notes_html:
Three main types of farming are practised in Pakistan, and the farming year is divided into two cropping seasons.

Small-Scale Subsistence Farming

  • Subsistence farming is farming mainly for household consumption; it is practised by approximately 90% of Pakistani farmers on landholdings smaller than 12.5 acres (5 hectares).
  • Despite their small holdings, subsistence farmers account for about 60% of the country's agricultural output, growing essential food crops such as wheat, rice and maize.
  • It relies heavily on manual labour — women and children help with animal feed, milking, eggs, poultry and harvesting — and on animal traction; tractors are rare because of poverty and small holdings.

Cash Crop (Commercial) Farming

  • Cash crop farming grows crops primarily for sale and profit, usually on extensive landholdings; examples are sugarcane, wheat, rice, corn, coffee, cocoa, soybeans, oilseeds, fruits and vegetables.
  • It employs a mix of skilled labour (machinery, pesticides, infrastructure) and unskilled labour (planting, weeding, harvesting).
  • Water is its biggest challenge: a network of dams and barrages stores Himalayan river water — the Tarbela Dam on the Indus and the Mangla Dam on the Jhelum are the two largest storage dams — and barrages like Sukkur and tubewells support irrigation where canals cannot reach.

Two Cropping Seasons

  • Kharif (summer): crops such as cotton and rice that thrive in high tropical temperatures.
  • Rabi (winter): crops such as wheat and rapeseed grown in the temperate winter of the lowlands.

Key Points

  • About 90% of farmers are subsistence farmers with under 12.5 acres, producing 60% of output.
  • Cash crops are grown for sale and profit on large holdings.
  • Kharif is the summer season (cotton, rice); Rabi is the winter season (wheat, rapeseed).

lessons.title: Major Crops: Cotton and Wheat
lessons.notes_html:
Cotton and wheat are Pakistan's most important cash and food crops respectively.

i. Cotton

  • Cotton is vital for both agriculture and the textile industry: it accounts for 0.6% of GDP and 3.1% of the value added in agriculture, and earns major foreign exchange through textile exports.
  • Requirements: moderate rainfall of about 1000 mm (or irrigation); temperatures between 25°C and 35°C (below 20°C stunts growth, above 40°C reduces yields); well-drained loamy soil with pH 6.0 to 7.5.
  • Problems: production is declining because cotton is less profitable than maize, paddy and sugarcane; whitefly and pink bollworm infestations; leaf curl virus; climate change, heat stress and extreme rainfall; excessive pesticide use; high input costs; and inadequate research into resistant varieties.
  • Revival measures: establish a minimum cotton price; expand agricultural extension services; develop pest-resistant (GM) cotton seeds; and introduce input subsidies through Kissan cards.

ii. Wheat

  • Wheat is Pakistan's primary staple crop and the key to food security; it contributes 9.2% to the value added in agriculture and 1.8% to GDP.
  • The 2021 wheat crop rose by 8.1% to a historic high of 27.293 million tonnes, up from 25.248 million tonnes the previous year, mainly through expansion of the cultivated area; high-yielding varieties such as Maxi Pak and MH-21 hold great potential.
  • Requirements: well-drained loamy soil, pH 6.0 to 7.5; moderate rainfall of 50 to 100 cm per year (or irrigation); cool-season temperatures of 10°C to 20°C (above 30°C stresses the crop).
  • Production areas: Punjab produces over 70% of Pakistan's wheat (Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh, Jhang, Chakwal); other areas are Jacobabad, Larkana and Shikarpur in Sindh, Mardan, Nowshera and Swabi in KPK, and Quetta, Pishin and Zhob in Balochistan.

Key Points

  • Cotton feeds the textile industry and exports but faces pests, virus and high costs.
  • Wheat is the main staple: 9.2% of agricultural value added, with Punjab growing over 70%.
  • Both crops need loamy soil and irrigation where rainfall is short.

lessons.title: Sugarcane, Rice, Maize and Other Crops
lessons.notes_html:
Besides cotton and wheat, Pakistan's major crops include sugarcane, rice, maize and tobacco, together with pulses, oilseeds and fruits.

iii. Sugarcane

  • Sugarcane contributes 3.4% to agriculture's value addition and 0.7% to GDP; in 2020-21 its area increased by 12% to 1,165 thousand hectares.
  • Requirements: rainfall of 100 to 1520 mm (or irrigation); well-drained loamy soil, pH 6.5 to 7.5; the land is tilled at least 30 cm deep, stalks are cut into 30-45 cm segments and planted in furrows 10-15 cm deep, spaced 75-100 cm apart; it needs regular irrigation, fertilization (especially potash) and a weed-free field.
  • Areas: Punjab produces over 60% (Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh, Jhang); Sindh follows (Jacobabad, Larkana, Shikarpur); KPK produces around 10% (Mardan, Nowshera, Swabi).

iv. Rice

  • Rice is the second most important staple after wheat and the second most exported commodity after cotton; it contributes 3.5% to agriculture's value-added and 0.7% to GDP. Its two types are Basmati (fine) and coarse rice; in 2020-21 it was cultivated on 3,335 thousand hectares.
  • Requirements: temperatures of 20°C to 35°C; rainfall of 100 to 250 cm per year (or irrigation); loamy soil, pH 6.5 to 7.5.
  • Cultivation: seedbed preparation, transplanting of 3-4 week old seedlings, regular irrigation, balanced fertilization every 4-6 weeks and weed control.
  • Areas: Punjab produces over 70% (Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh, Sialkot, Gujranwala); Sindh about 20%; KPK about 10%; Balochistan's rice cultivation is limited.
  • Challenges and management: pests and diseases (stem borers, brown plant hoppers, blast), abiotic stresses (drought, salinity, flooding), weeds and nutrient deficiency; managed through pest and disease control, laser levelling, drip irrigation, alternate wetting and drying (AWD) and nutrient management.

v. Maize and vi. Tobacco

  • Maize is the third-leading cereal crop after wheat and rice, contributing 3.4% to value-added and 0.6% to GDP; it is used for corn flour and custard powder and, increasingly, for livestock and poultry feed and wet milling; in 2020-21 it covered 1,418 thousand hectares.
  • Tobacco is concentrated in Swabi, Mardan, Nowshera and Charsadda, which produce over 90% of the country's Flue-Cured Virginia (FCV) tobacco; it is grown by transplanting seedlings or direct sowing and demands intensive labour, including curing of the leaves.

Other Crops and Fruit Farming

  • Other crops include bajra, jawar, gram, barley, rapeseed and mustard, and pulses such as moong and mash; Pakistan imported 2.917 million tonnes of edible oil in FY 2021 against domestic production of only 0.374 million tonnes.
  • Fruit farming is practised in all four provinces: Punjab is the largest fruit producer (over 60% — Multan, Faisalabad, Toba Tek Singh, Sargodha), Sindh second (about 25%), KPK third (about 10%); Hunza and Swat are renowned for apples and apricots, and Balochistan produces apples, dates, apricots and grapes; Pakistan is also a leading producer of dry fruits such as almonds, walnuts and raisins.
  • The government supports fruit farmers with subsidies for plants and fertilizers and training in modern practices.

Key Points

  • Sugarcane and rice each add about 0.7% to GDP; Punjab leads in both.
  • Maize is the third cereal; FCV tobacco is concentrated in four KPK districts.
  • Punjab also leads fruit production with over 60% of the national total.

lessons.title: Livestock Farming
lessons.notes_html:
Livestock farming — raising domesticated animals for meat, milk, eggs and other products — is one of the oldest and most significant forms of agriculture. It contributes around 11% to GDP and employs over 35 million people, ensuring food security. There are three types of livestock farming in Pakistan.

Nomadic Livestock Farming

  • Herders move their animals from place to place in search of pasture and water.
  • It is prevalent in arid and semi-arid regions with limited resources, among the Baloch and Pashtun tribes of Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; sheep and goats are the primary species.

Settled Livestock Farming

  • Animals are kept in permanent enclosures in areas with abundant arable land and water.
  • It is practised throughout Pakistan, concentrated in Punjab and Sindh; the main animals are cattle, buffaloes, goats and poultry.

Transhumance

  • Herders move their animals between different pastures according to the seasons, in mountainous regions where pasture availability changes through the year.
  • The Gujjar and Bakarwal tribes of the Kashmir region practise transhumance, mainly raising sheep and goats.

Organic Farming Methods

  • Crop rotation — planting different crops in sequence, with one patch left fallow to rest — improves soil fertility and reduces pests and diseases.
  • Intercropping grows two or more crops in the same field at the same time; cover cropping covers the soil surface and prevents erosion.
  • Composting makes compost from plant residues, manure and food scraps.
  • Biological pest control uses natural predators — for example ladybugs against aphids and lacewings against whiteflies.
  • Farmland must not be converted into housing schemes, and more water schemes help sustain agricultural activities.

Key Points

  • Livestock adds about 11% to GDP and employs over 35 million people.
  • Nomadic farming moves with pasture; settled farming keeps animals in enclosures; transhumance moves with the seasons.
  • Organic methods include rotation, intercropping, cover cropping, composting and biological pest control.

lessons.title: Fisheries
lessons.notes_html:
Fisheries is the industry or activity of catching or raising fish. Fishing is a major industry in Pakistan's coastal communities, and the fishing sector employs approximately 2 million people as fishermen, processors and traders.

Marine and Inland Fishing

  • Marine fishing is done in the Arabian Sea along the Sindh and Makran coasts, using trawlers, gill nets and long lines from boats.
  • Fishing ports on the Sindh coast include Karachi Fish Harbour, Ibrahim Hyderi and Keti Bunder; on the Makran coast are Gwadar, Pasni, Ormara and Jiwani.
  • Important fish species of the Balochistan coast include tuna, sardines and mackerels; the sector needs better port and processing infrastructure, and the coastal highway and Gwadar port can revitalise it.
  • Inland fishing uses nets, ponds and fish farms in rivers, lakes and dams, where fish such as rohu and catla are raised and caught. Developing fish farms in the Indus plain using abandoned river channels or canal water can add income and protein and reduce the burden on crops and livestock.

Fish Farming: Inland Farming and Aquaculture

  • Aquaculture is the farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, shellfish and seaweed.
  • Inland fish farming is practised in freshwater bodies and typically involves smaller-scale operations, while aquaculture can be practised in both freshwater and saltwater bodies and at small or large scale.
  • Both involve farming aquatic organisms, produce food for human consumption and provide income and employment.

Problems and Protection

  • The biggest challenges facing the fishing sector are overfishing — catching fish faster than the population can reproduce — fishing of endangered species and water pollution.
  • Fishery management — managing fish populations and their habitats — ensures sustainable fishing.
  • Protective measures include controlling overfishing, banning harmful nets, protecting fish breeding grounds and mangroves, and providing cold storage, modern boats, training and fair prices to raise fishermen's income and exports.

Key Points

  • Fisheries employ about 2 million people along the Sindh and Makran coasts and inland waters.
  • Marine fishing uses trawlers, gill nets and long lines; inland fishing uses ponds and farms.
  • Overfishing, endangered-species fishing and pollution are the main threats; management keeps fishing sustainable.

lessons.title: Transport and Regional Variations in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Transport is the movement of people, products or animals from one location to another. It is a key part of human activity and of economic systems, and it involves the physical transfer of humans or objects over different distances. The primary modes of transport are road, rail, air, maritime, space, pipeline and cable transport, and each mode serves a distinct purpose.

Transport in Pakistan

  • In Pakistan, the types of transport used depend mainly on topography, population and economic activity.
  • Modes are also chosen by their purpose — public transport systems, supply of goods, and short-distance travel within cities and towns.
  • Distance, speed, cost, volume and the type of items or passengers being carried all influence which mode of transport is used.

Regional Variations in Transport Services

  • Pakistan has a varied landscape of mountains, plains, deserts and rivers, and the terrain affects how easy and how costly it is to build transport infrastructure.
  • In steep or inaccessible areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, local chairlifts carry passengers and goods across rivers and hills, and animals are used during hiking and trekking.
  • Transport is in greater demand in crowded places, so population distribution shapes the transport network.
  • Economic activity is unevenly spread — regions with more industry and trade have more developed transport to support commerce and trade.
  • Extreme weather and climate can also force people to use alternative types of transport.

Key Points

  • Transport means moving people, goods or animals from one place to another.
  • The main modes are road, rail, air, maritime, space, pipeline and cable transport.
  • Topography, population and economic activity decide the transport used in each region of Pakistan.

lessons.title: Road Transport
lessons.notes_html:
Road transport is the principal form of transport for people and products in Pakistan. It connects cities, towns and rural areas through motorways, highways, roads of strategic importance, roads linking villages and towns, and roads within cities. Road travel is the most common mode of travel in the country.

The Road Network

  • According to the Pakistan Economic Survey 2022-23, the National Highway Authority (NHA) network has 48 national highways, motorways and key roads totalling 14,480 km.
  • The NHA network is only 4.6% of the total national road network of about 263,775 km, yet it carries 80% of commercial traffic.
  • National Highway N-5, running from Karachi to Torkham, is called the bloodline of Pakistan — it alone carries 65% of the traffic load of the country.
  • Other important highways are the Indus Highway (N-55) and the Karakoram Highway (N-35); busy motorways include M-2 (Islamabad to Lahore), M-9 (Hyderabad to Karachi) and M-1 (Peshawar to Islamabad), which greatly reduce travel time.
  • Punjab has the largest share of the road network because it is the centre of economic activity and population. As of May 2019, 25,238,000 vehicles were registered in Pakistan.

Advantages of Road Transport

  • It is widely accessible, reaching urban and rural areas and even isolated places.
  • It is flexible in routes and cargo types, allows quick delivery of time-critical goods, and provides the last-mile connection to the final destination.
  • It supports economic activity in less accessible areas and is convenient for passengers through buses, taxis and private vehicles.
  • It is critical for emergency response — ambulances and fire trucks can travel quickly.

Disadvantages of Road Transport

  • It is not cost-effective for very long distances, and road accidents endanger people and goods — road transport has the most security and safety concerns of all modes.
  • There are risks of theft or damage, roads need constant maintenance, and floods and landslides can block supply routes.
  • Traffic congestion in big cities causes delays and higher costs, while vehicles add to air pollution and dependence on fossil fuels.

Key Points

  • Road transport is Pakistan's main and most common mode of travel.
  • The NHA network of 14,480 km carries 80% of commercial traffic; N-5 alone carries 65% of the traffic load.
  • Roads are flexible and door-to-door, but suffer from accidents, congestion and pollution.

lessons.title: Rail Transport
lessons.notes_html:
Rail transport is an efficient and cost-effective way of moving people and commodities across Pakistan. Pakistan Railways operates the rail network for both freight and passenger travel, and the network plays a vital role in national integration and economic prosperity.

The Railway Network

  • Pakistan Railways has a route length of 7,791 km.
  • The primary rail lines are ML-1 and ML-2, along with smaller branch lines that connect other areas.
  • Intercity trains connect the major cities and give passengers a comfortable and reasonably quick form of travel; some trains run as express or non-stop services, which shortens travel time between important cities.
  • With modern facilities in trains and upgradation of lines and other infrastructure, this mode of transport can be further improved.

Advantages of Rail Transport

  • Rail is more cost-effective than road transport for long-distance movement of commodities.
  • Trains can carry vast amounts of bulk material, making them ideal for industries such as mining and agriculture.
  • Trains use less fuel than road vehicles, which saves money and benefits the environment; they also emit fewer pollutants.
  • Rail travel reduces traffic congestion and is generally safer, with fewer accidents and deaths.
  • Rail infrastructure is more stable than roads, so bad weather affects it less, and corridor projects such as CPEC improve connectivity and trade ties.

Disadvantages of Rail Transport

  • Rail networks have limited access to isolated or underdeveloped areas, so people there must rely on other modes.
  • Trains can be slow for short distances because of loading, unloading and possible transhipment time.
  • Rail runs on fixed routes, so it is less flexible than road transport.
  • Unlike road transport, rail does not provide door-to-door service — extra transport is needed for the first and last parts of the journey.

Key Points

  • Pakistan Railways runs a 7,791 km network; ML-1 and ML-2 are the main lines.
  • Rail is cheap, safe and fuel-efficient for bulk goods over long distances.
  • Its weaknesses are fixed routes, limited reach and no door-to-door service.

lessons.title: Air Transport and Dry Ports
lessons.notes_html:
Air transport is provided in Pakistan mainly by Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), the national flag carrier, which has a fleet of 35 aircraft. Private Pakistani airlines and well-known international airlines also carry passengers and freight to and from Pakistan.

Airports of Pakistan

  • Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad airports are the busiest in Pakistan, connecting many national and international destinations.
  • Sialkot airport facilitates business people travelling to and from Sialkot, while Gilgit, Skardu and Chitral airports connect the northern areas and bring in local and international visitors.

Advantages of Air Transport

  • Air travel is the quickest means of transport, moving people and cargo speedily over great distances and giving international connectivity.
  • It is ideal for high-value and time-sensitive cargo, such as perishable goods and urgent shipments.
  • It overcomes physical barriers — mountains, rivers and difficult terrain — that block other modes.
  • It supports business travel, diplomacy and tourism, and is crucial for emergency medical services, carrying patients and medical supplies quickly.

Dry Ports of Pakistan

  • Dry ports are inland facilities that provide logistics and storage services linked to seaports, airports and other transport hubs; they simplify the movement of goods for export.
  • The most important dry ports are at Lahore, Karachi, Islamabad, Faisalabad, Sialkot, Quetta, Multan, Rawalpindi and Gujranwala. The Wagah dry port facilitates trade with India and transit trade with Afghanistan and Central Asia.
  • Sialkot dry port serves the export of sports goods, surgical instruments, leather goods and textiles; Faisalabad dry port serves textiles, chemicals, engineering goods and agricultural products.
  • Dry ports bring customs clearance, documentation and cargo handling close to factories, which cuts transit time and cost, reduces pressure on seaports and makes Pakistan's exports more competitive.

Key Points

  • PIA, with 35 aircraft, is the national flag carrier; Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad are the busiest airports.
  • Air transport is the fastest mode and best for urgent, perishable and high-value goods.
  • Dry ports provide inland customs and cargo facilities that speed up exports and relieve the seaports.

lessons.title: Trade and Its Role in Pakistan's Economy
lessons.notes_html:
Trade is the exchange of products and services between individuals, businesses or countries. It is a basic economic activity that has been part of human societies for generations — one party gives commodities or services in exchange for something of value, such as money, other items or services. Pakistan's trade includes both exports and imports.

Role of Trade in the Economy of Pakistan

  • Trade, particularly exports, is a significant part of Pakistan's GDP — in 2022, trade was reported at 32.32% of the total GDP.
  • Exporting goods and services generates revenue and contributes to overall economic output and growth.
  • International trade gives Pakistan access to global markets, so its products reach consumers all over the world, which improves the competitiveness of Pakistani goods and services.
  • Through trade agreements and membership of organisations such as the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Pakistan gains preferential access to foreign markets, with lower trade barriers and tariffs.
  • Foreign exchange reserves are strengthened by export earnings; these reserves keep the external sector stable, finance imports and meet international obligations.
  • A large part of the population works in trade-related sectors such as export manufacturing, transportation and logistics; export-oriented industries like textiles and clothing create many jobs.
  • International trade also brings new technologies and innovations into Pakistan, transferring knowledge and skills that improve local technology.
  • Pakistan's major exports include textiles, rice, leather goods, sports goods and surgical instruments, while major imports include petroleum, machinery, chemicals and edible oil. When the value of imports exceeds exports, the country faces a trade deficit.

Key Points

  • Trade is the exchange of goods and services for money or other value.
  • In 2022 trade equalled 32.32% of Pakistan's GDP.
  • Trade earns foreign exchange, creates jobs, opens global markets and brings new technology.

lessons.title: Trade Routes, Factors and Internal Challenges
lessons.notes_html:
Because of its geographical location, Pakistan is a crucial junction for many trade routes, linking it with China, Central Asia and the Middle East. Pakistan's largest trading partner is China.

Important Trade Routes

RouteLink
Karachi Port and Port QasimMajor seaports handling most of Pakistan's marine traffic
Gwadar Port and CPECDeep-sea port in Balochistan; links Central Asia and the Middle East
Wagah BorderTrade route between Pakistan and India
Peshawar-Torkham HighwayLand route to Afghanistan and Central Asia; carries transit trade
Quetta-Chaman RouteLand route to Afghanistan; gateway to Central Asia
Karakoram Highway (KKH)Part of CPEC; land route connecting Pakistan and China
Taftan-Mirjavah CrossingMain border crossing between Pakistan and Iran

Factors Affecting International Trade

  • Economic stability: stable economies trade more; currency fluctuations change export and import prices and competitiveness.
  • Customs and documentation: long or complicated customs processes slow the flow of goods; ease of doing business improves trade.
  • Political stability: stable countries attract investors and traders; turmoil and conflict disrupt trade, as Pakistan has experienced.
  • Trade agreements: agreements lower tariffs and open markets. Pakistan is a member of the WTO and SAFTA; the EU has given Pakistan GSP+ status (till 2027, extendable) with duty-free access to the EU market; and the bilateral agreement with China is the China-Pakistan Free Trade Agreement (CPFTA).
  • Transport and communication: good infrastructure lowers the cost and time of trade — CPEC road improvements are an example.
  • Global economy and market demand: downturns reduce demand; after Covid, world trade and business dipped sharply.

Internal Challenges

  • Infrastructure challenges: inadequate and outdated roads, ports and trains impede the movement of goods.
  • Energy problems: power shortages reduce industrial efficiency and exports; cutting circular debt and investing in alternate and hydel energy can help.
  • Logistics and trade facilitation: slow customs clearance and documentation raise costs; one-window operations can improve this.
  • Bureaucratic obstacles, unstable financial policies and lack of skilled labour reduce competitiveness; technical and vocational education should be preferred.
  • Security concerns and corruption discourage international businesses and investors; transparency, anti-corruption measures and good governance are needed to restore trader confidence.

Key Points

  • Karachi Port, Port Qasim and Gwadar handle sea trade; Wagah, Torkham, Chaman, Taftan and the KKH are the main land routes.
  • Trade is shaped by economic and political stability, agreements such as CPFTA and GSP+, transport and global demand.
  • Weak infrastructure, energy shortage, red tape, skill shortage, insecurity and corruption are Pakistan's main internal challenges.
